entry.content:
The advisory

On 2026-11-18 the Ruby team published a security advisory for seven vulnerabilities in the regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings, and released Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10 to fix them. One of the seven is GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, now CVE-2026-132825, rated CVSS 7.4. You may have seen it under the name Ruby2Shell. The advisory gives it three sentences: Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings, changing the case of a crafted string “may allow remote code execution”, and the Ruby team is aware of PoCs that reach it in some scenarios. It affects every Ruby up to 3.3.13, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. It does not say which string, which method or which encoding, and when I checked on 2026-11-19 no public PoC code existed.

So I set out to find the string, starting from the fix commit. It turned out to be 21 bytes long. One HTTP request with no credentials, carrying 21 copies of the byte 0xDF and a Content-Type that declares ISO-8859-1, makes Ruby 3.4.12 write one byte past the end of a heap buffer inside a Sinatra application. The proof is the target’s own AddressSanitizer report, the same request is answered correctly by Ruby 3.4.13, and the run is in a live pcap.

That is a lower impact than the advisory describes, and I want to be plain about it from the first screen. I did not reach remote code execution. This post explains the bug, the quiet byte, what the same request does without the sanitizer, and where I stopped.

PoC, detection rules, and live pcap: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-132825

A letter that grows

Every Ruby string carries an encoding. Today that is almost always UTF-8, Ruby’s default, and nothing in this post applies to UTF-8 strings. But Ruby still ships the legacy single-byte encodings: ISO-8859-1 through -16 and the Windows-125x code pages. Each has a small C file under enc/, and each of those files has a function called case_map that knows how to turn that encoding’s letters into upper case, lower case, title case or folded case.

In a single-byte encoding, changing case is almost always one byte in, one byte out. The exception is the German sharp s, ß, which sits at byte 0xDF in fourteen of these encodings. Its upper-case form is two letters, SS. One byte in, two bytes out. The PoC’s baseline request shows this on the live target before anything bad happens:

Six bytes in, seven out. That growth is why Ruby cannot change case in place. String#upcase ends up in rb_str_casemap in string.c, which allocates a separate output buffer, a mapping_buffer: a 24-byte header (capa, used, next) followed by the output space. The space is sized as the remaining input length plus 20, a constant named CASE_MAPPING_ADDITIONAL_LENGTH. Twenty spare bytes cover twenty sharp s. If the output grows more than that, the encoding’s case_map is expected to stop when the buffer is full, and rb_str_casemap links another buffer for the rest. That is what the next field is for.

The whole design rests on one promise: case_map stops before the end of the buffer. The last line of that excerpt says the baseline fits in a 26-byte buffer. The interesting question is what happens when it does not.

The vulnerable code

The fix commit says more than the advisory does. It is titled “Fix a heap buffer overflow in case mapping of the sharp s”, and it changes the same line in fourteen encoding files. Here is the loop it touches, from enc/iso_8859_1.c in Ruby 3.4.12, abridged, with my comments. The other thirteen files have the same pattern.

to is the write position and to_end is one past the last byte of the buffer. The loop condition to < to_end asks: is there room for one more byte? For every character except one, that is the right question. For the sharp s under upcase, the body writes S at line 272, sets code to the second letter, and falls through to the common store at line 293. Two writes after a check for one.

So if the loop is entered with exactly one byte free and the next input byte is 0xDF, the first S takes the last byte of the buffer and the second one lands at to_end, one byte past the allocation. It is a textbook off-by-one, CWE-193, and the same loop sits in fourteen files: enc/iso_8859_{1,2,3,4,9,10,13,14,15,16}.c and enc/windows_{1250,1252,1254,1257}.c.

The same shape exists for the other operations that expand a sharp s. swapcase writes SS as well. downcase(:fold) writes ss. capitalize writes Ss for a leading sharp s. casecmp? folds its operands, so it goes through the same code. That gives five affected methods, plus their bang forms, and two possible values for the stray byte: S (0x53) or s (0x73).

Notice what the attacker does not get. The byte past the buffer is never an input byte. It is a letter the encoding table chose.

Counting to forty-one

The overflow needs the loop to arrive at a sharp s with exactly one byte free. Whether that happens is pure arithmetic on the input.

Take an input of n bytes. The first buffer has n + 20 bytes of output space. Every ordinary byte advances the write position by one, every sharp s by two. Say j ordinary bytes and k sharp s have been processed when the fatal sharp s comes up. One byte free means j + 2k = n + 19.

The fatal character is itself part of the input, so n is at least j + k + 1. Put that into the equation and k comes out as at least 20. In other words: the twenty spare bytes have to be used up by twenty sharp s before the twenty-first can do damage. No ordinary sentence does that. A crafted string does it trivially.

The smallest case has no ordinary bytes at all. With j = 0 the equation is 2k = n + 19, so n must be odd, and the smallest n that leaves room for the fatal character is 21. Twenty-one sharp s get a 41-byte output space. Twenty of them fill offsets 0 to 39. The twenty-first enters the loop at offset 40, where 40 < 41 holds, and writes S at 40 and S at 41. Offset 41 does not exist.

An all-sharp-s string of even length never hits the condition: the output space is even too, the write position moves in steps of two, and it goes from two bytes free straight to full without ever standing on the last byte. Mixed strings fix the parity. Seven a followed by 21 sharp s is 28 bytes and overflows just the same, and that particular shape matters later.

With the 24-byte header, the 21-byte input turns into a malloc request for 65 bytes, and the stray S is byte number 66.

A door

Ruby is a language runtime, so this bug needs a host: some application that takes text from the network, holds it in one of the fourteen encodings and changes its case. The advisory names none, so the lab uses the smallest honest stand-in I could write: a Sinatra 4.2.2 service on Puma 8.1.2 that upper-cases whatever a client posts, in the character set the client declares. This is the whole handler, from lab/app/app.rb:

There is no memory-unsafe code here. The application reads the body, labels it with the declared encoding, rejects byte sequences that are invalid in that encoding, and calls upcase. In ISO-8859-1 every byte is a valid character, so 21 bytes of 0xDF pass the check as the perfectly legal string ßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßßß.

Treat this application as a lab deviation and judge it as one. Trusting the client’s charset parameter is a design choice I made so that one request is enough. A real target has to do two things on its own: hold attacker-controlled text in one of these encodings, and call one of the five methods on it. An application whose strings stay in UTF-8 does not take this code path.

Two details in Ruby itself narrow the path a little further. A string with only 7-bit characters in a single-byte encoding takes a fast path in rb_str_upcase and never reaches case_map, so plain ASCII is not a trigger. And a call with the :ascii option does not reach it either.

The trigger, as the PoC sent it:

No cookie, no token, no session. 186 bytes on the wire.

One byte is quiet

Here is the part the advisory does not prepare you for. Send that request to a stock Ruby 3.4.12 and you get a polite 200. I checked that later, against a build without the sanitizer, and there is a section on it below. The overflow happens. Nothing notices.

A one-byte write past a 65-byte allocation lands in memory that the allocator rounded up and nobody uses. No crash, no log line, no changed response. A proof that says “the heap is corrupted, trust me” is not a proof, so the lab builds Ruby with AddressSanitizer, which surrounds every allocation with poisoned memory and reports the first access that touches it.

Both lab images are built from the official release tarballs, checksum-pinned, with clang 19 and the recipe from Ruby’s own doc/contributing/building_ruby.md: cflags='-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -DUSE_MN_THREADS=0'. The source is not patched. The only difference between the two images is the tarball: 3.4.12, the last vulnerable release of its series, and 3.4.13, the first fixed one. During setup each image prints the loop guard it was compiled from, so the run itself shows which code is under test: while (*pp < end && to < to_end) { in one, while (*pp < end && to_end - to > 1) { in the other.

One more setting is mine: abort_on_error=1 in ASAN_OPTIONS, so that the sanitizer ends the process with abort() and the container’s exit status names the signal. That changes how the sanitizer dies, not what it detects.

Keep in mind what this means for everything in the next section. The abort you are about to see is the sanitizer’s. It is the instrument, not the bug’s natural behaviour.

The report

The request above never got an answer. This is the target’s own log, evidence/target-vuln-asan.txt, with my cuts marked:

Read it in three parts.

The first block is the write. WRITE of size 1, in case_map, at enc/iso_8859_1.c:293. That is the common store from the listing above, the second byte of SS. It was called from rb_str_casemap, which was called from rb_str_upcase.

The second block is the victim. The address is “0 bytes after” a 65-byte region, and that region was allocated by rb_str_casemap at string.c:7834, inside the same upcase call. Sixty-five is the 24-byte header plus 41 bytes of output space, exactly what the arithmetic predicted. The region ends at 0x50700021c331 and the write is at 0x50700021c331.

The shadow bytes show the same thing as a picture. Each shadow byte describes eight bytes of real memory. The buffer starts sixteen bytes before the marked row, which is the 00 00 at the end of the row above. Then come six more 00, 48 fully usable bytes, and then [01]: a group of eight in which only the first byte may be touched. Sixteen plus 48 plus one is 65. Everything after it is fa, redzone. The brackets mark the group the write hit: it went for the second byte of a group that has one.

The third block is Ruby’s own crash handler, and it closes the chain from the network to the C function. /app/app.rb:41 is the text.upcase line of the handler. The control frames show CFUNC :upcase called from a block in app.rb, and the Ruby-level backtrace in the full log runs from Puma’s thread pool through Sinatra’s route dispatch down to those last two lines. This is the request handler, running my request.

From the outside, the same moment looks like this (evidence/poc-vuln.txt):

Exit code 134 is SIGABRT, and oom_killed=false rules out the kernel’s out-of-memory killer. In the capture, the trigger request is packet #24 at 07:32:44.765917 on the lab host’s clock, which ran about 60 seconds ahead of the clock behind the “sent” line above. The target closes the connection 539 ms later without having sent a byte, and later connection attempts are reset. The script that printed these lines never had a shell on the target: with --container it reads the stopped container’s log and state afterwards, which is evidence collection, not part of the attack.

The overflow depends only on the request bytes, so it is deterministic. One request, one report.

Negative control

Same script, same request, same application, Ruby 3.4.13 (evidence/poc-patched.txt):

Forty-two S, the correct answer, and a server that is still there. The response is also a small demonstration of the buffer chain doing its job: 42 bytes of output cannot fit in a 41-byte space, so the fixed loop must have stopped after twenty sharp s and left the last one to a second buffer.

Without the sanitizer

I did not want to leave it at “ASAN says so”, because a sanitizer build is not what anyone runs in production. So I rebuilt the vulnerable image with the sanitizer flags removed and nothing else changed, and pointed the unmodified PoC at it.

A warning first: the runs in this section are not in the repository’s evidence set. The repository ships the smallest set of files that proves its claims, and these are not among them. Read this section as lab notes.

The default 21-byte request did nothing, 200 times in a row. Every one was answered with a 200.

The reason is in how glibc sizes its chunks. The lab’s glibc is 2.41. For a 65-byte request it hands out a chunk with 72 usable bytes, so byte number 66 falls into seven bytes of slack that belong to the same chunk. Harmless.

Change the input length and the picture changes. A 28-byte input makes the request 72 bytes, the chunk has no slack at all, and byte number 73 is the first byte of whatever comes next in memory. In glibc that is the size field of the next chunk. This is where the seven a plus 21 sharp s from earlier come in: poc.py --prefix 7 --count 21 sends exactly that shape.

The stray byte overwrites the low byte of that size field, which is also where glibc keeps its flag bits. In a small simulation with the same glibc, a neighbour whose size field read 0x51 came out as 0x53 or 0x73, and both values set the flag that says “this chunk came from mmap”. Nothing happens at that moment. Later, when the program frees the neighbour, glibc treats it as a mapped chunk, finds that it is not a valid one, prints munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer and aborts.

Over HTTP, against the stock build, that is what I saw. In the first container the 74th request got no answer and the process was gone with SIGABRT and that message at the end of its log. Three more fresh containers went the same way after 976, 967 and 925 requests. All the requests before the fatal one were answered correctly. A bare Ruby script that made the same upcase call 2000 times on the lab’s stock binary survived, while an earlier probe with the same script in the official ruby:3.4.12-slim image aborted with the same message. Whether the damaged neighbour is ever freed depends on the heap layout, and a web server’s heap frees a lot.

Other input lengths hit different glibc integrity checks. At eight lengths from 21 to 1004 bytes, five produced crashes through three distinct abort modes: the munmap_chunk path above, mismatching next->prev_size during unsorted-bin processing, and corrupted size vs. prev_size during forward consolidation. Controls without the overflow survived every time. Warmup requests on the same connection changed which chunk sat next to the mapping buffer — the heap layout is not static, and HTTP requests influence it.

If you try this yourself, know that the shipped poc.py does not count it as a hit. It attributes a stop to the bug only when it finds a sanitizer report, and against a stock build it prints RESULT: not confirmed: the stop is not attributed to the overflow (exit 1). That is deliberate. A dead process alone is not proof of this bug, and the repository’s claims stay with the sanitizer build, where the target itself names the function and the line.

What one byte buys

What I can prove is narrow and solid: a pre-authentication, single-request, one-byte out-of-bounds heap write in the Ruby runtime, reached over the network through an ordinary web stack, with the target-side report and a negative control.

What the advisory describes is more: remote code execution. The Ruby team says PoCs exist that reach it in some scenarios, and I have no reason to doubt them. I did not get there. Here is what stood in the way from where I stopped.

The value is fixed. The byte is S or s, chosen by the method the application calls, not by the attacker.

The position is fixed. It is always the first byte past the mapping buffer. The attacker chooses the input length, and with it the size class the buffer is allocated from. Nothing else.

There is no read side. The HTTP response is copied out of the mapping buffer within bounds, and no code path returns the stray byte or anything near it.

So the byte lands on allocator bookkeeping, with a value the attacker does not choose, and nothing comes back. The exploitation mechanism itself — forward consolidation creating an overlapping allocation — was validated in a probe on the same glibc with the actual byte 0x53, so the primitive is mechanically sound. But through this endpoint I got a process abort and nothing more. HTTP warmup requests do change which chunk sits next to the mapping buffer, so heap layout is not entirely out of reach. What is missing is the critical piece: an address leak. The endpoint returns only the uppercased text, and no path was found that exposes heap data. Without addresses, nothing can be aimed.

ClaimStatusEvidence
The 21 × 0xDF ISO-8859-1 request makes Ruby 3.4.12 write one byte past a heap buffer in case_map (enc/iso_8859_1.c:293), reached through String#upcase in the request handlerProvenevidence/poc-vuln.txt, evidence/target-vuln-asan.txt
The request arrives over HTTP with no credentials, and nothing else is done to the targetProvencapture/exploit.pcap (packet #24), poc.py
The sanitizer build aborts (SIGABRT, exit 134) and the service goes downProvenevidence/poc-vuln.txt; capture packets #26 and #36 to #44
Ruby 3.4.13 handles the same request correctlyConfirmed (negative control run)evidence/poc-patched.txt
Remote code execution against the productNot reachedno command ran on the target. Tried through the product: the trigger against the sanitizer build (abort) and repeated requests at eight input lengths against a stock build (three distinct glibc abort modes at five of them, lab notes above). The exploitation mechanism (forward consolidation to overlapping allocation) was validated with the actual byte 0x53 in a probe on the same glibc, not through the product. The endpoint returns only the uppercased text; no path was found that leaks heap data or addresses. HTTP warmup requests change which chunk sits next to the mapping buffer, but not what that chunk contains. Gaps: the fixed byte value, the absent info leak (the critical one), and no mechanism to place attacker-controlled bytes in the corrupted neighbour
The other 13 encodings and the other four methodsNot reachednot run; the fix diff shows the same pattern in all 14 files, and poc.py --charset selects another encoding

“Not reached” describes where this work stopped. It is not a statement about the bug.

I tested one Ruby series (3.4), one encoding (ISO-8859-1), one method (upcase) and one application, on x86_64 Linux.

Detection

The repository has two Suricata rules and one Sigma rule. All three are experimental / minimally validated: each was tested only against the attack capture or target log from this lab and one benign sample. I make no claim about coverage or false-positive rates.

The first Suricata rule looks for the two things the request cannot do without, a legacy charset and a run of sharp s:

It fired once on capture/exploit.pcap, on the trigger request, and stayed silent on a benign request that posts a word with a single sharp s to the same endpoint. The second rule, sid 1000002, is the same with windows-125 as the charset. It loads cleanly and was silent on the benign sample, but it has not fired on anything, because my capture uses ISO-8859-1.

The limits are easy to state. The rules need plaintext HTTP or TLS termination in front of the sensor. They match 21 consecutive 0xDF bytes, and the arithmetic above shows that the sharp s do not have to be consecutive: a payload that spreads them among other characters still overflows and is not matched. And HTTP is only one way to hand text to a Ruby program.

The Sigma rule watches the Ruby process output for the crash: heap-buffer-overflow together with case_map, or [BUG] ASAN error together with upcase, or glibc’s munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer. The first two match the log of the vulnerable run and not the patched one. The third is there for builds without a sanitizer; it has no sample in the repository and it will fire on any heap corruption glibc catches that way, whatever the cause. Details are in detection/README.md.

The fix

The fix is one line, fourteen times:

to_end - to > 1 means: enter the loop only when two bytes are free. That is the most any single character in these encodings can produce, so no iteration can overrun. The cost is that the loop now sometimes stops with one byte unused, and rb_str_casemap links another buffer a little earlier than it strictly had to. The negative control above is consistent with exactly that.

The commit also adds a test that walks all fourteen encodings and every length from 1 to 64 through upcase, downcase(:fold), swapcase, capitalize and casecmp?. Ruby 3.4.13 fixes several advisories at once, so I also diffed the 3.4.12 and 3.4.13 tarballs to make sure the lab compares what I think it compares: all fourteen files carry the same one-line change.

The Ruby team’s recommendation is to upgrade to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

Advisory and fix

DateEvent
2026-10-28Fix commit b841d6f authored, “Fix a heap buffer overflow in case mapping of the sharp s”
2026-11-18Ruby security advisory posted; Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10 released
2026-11-20Reproduction and write-up

Advisory: Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion and GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5. The advisory credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with the report. No CVSS vector has been published; the 7.4 score comes from external sources, and the GitHub advisory labels the bug Critical.

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in the table from the repository. You need Python 3.8 or later and Docker with BuildKit on an x86_64 Linux host. The first run compiles Ruby twice with the sanitizer, which takes a few minutes.

The raw output of every run quoted here, the capture and the rules are in the repository: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-132825.
entry.summary: CVE-2026-132825: one-byte heap overflow in Ruby's String#upcase on ISO-8859-x text, CVSS 7.4. Reproduced over HTTP with a PoC, ASAN proof, pcap and rules.
entry.title: CVE-2026-132825: One Sharp S Too Many -- A One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby's Case Conversion

entry.content:
The advisory

Oracle’s November 2026 Critical Patch Update lists CVE-2026-114938 under the HotSpot compiler component: exploitable over the network with no credentials, high attack complexity, “takeover”, CVSS 8.1. The reporter nicknamed it Java4Shell and describes pre-auth remote code execution through heap grooming, with the exploit chains withheld, plus a heap memory disclosure. The affected code is the Base64 decoder of the Java runtime itself, in OpenJDK builds of the 17, 21, 25 and 27 lines from before the November 2026 update, on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. Any Java service on such a machine that decodes Base64 from the network is exposed, and that starts with HTTP Basic authentication.

I wanted to see what the bug does to a real product that nobody prepared for it. The answer: an unmodified Jenkins 2.580.2 LTS on Amazon Corretto 21.0.13.0.11, default JVM flags, dies with SIGSEGV after HTTP requests that carry no credentials at all. The JVM’s own fatal error report shows the decoder’s constant bytes sitting where a class pointer should be, the same script does nothing to the first fixed build, and the crashing run is in a live pcap. Against Jenkins I did not reach code execution or heap disclosure. In the lab, inside a single test JVM on the same vulnerable build, I did drive the same overflow to a redirected method call that runs /usr/bin/id. That chain is in-process and ends in a stand-in gadget I wrote myself, so it shows that the bug is a code-execution primitive, not that Jenkins can be attacked that way over the network. This post says exactly how far I got and what stands in the way.

PoC, detection rule, and live pcap: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-114938

Where Base64 turns into assembly

java.util.Base64 is one of those classes that every Java service touches without thinking about it. HTTP Basic authentication is Base64. So are many tokens, upload formats and message envelopes. When a server receives Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz, something calls Base64.getDecoder().decode() on bytes that came straight off the network, and it does so before it can possibly know who is asking.

The Java side is simple. Decoder.decode(byte[]) computes how many bytes the input will produce, allocates an array of exactly that size, and hands both to decode0:

Inside decode0 the real work happens in decodeBlock, a plain loop that turns four characters into three bytes. That loop is marked as an intrinsic candidate. When HotSpot’s optimizing compiler, C2, compiles decode0, it does not compile the Java loop. It replaces the call with a hand-written assembly stub tuned for the CPU the JVM is running on.

On x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Intel Ice Lake and later Xeon, AMD Zen 4 and later) that stub works on 64 characters at a time in 512-bit registers. ARM64 and CPUs without VBMI are not affected. The stub lives in StubGenerator::generate_base64_decodeBlock() in src/hotspot/cpu/x86/stubGenerator_x86_64.cpp, and it is only used where decode0 runs as C2 code. The interpreter, the C1 compiler and a standalone compiled decodeBlock all use the Java loop. That detail matters later.

One more property matters: the stub has no idea how big the destination array is. The Java documentation of decodeBlock says so directly: no length check is possible on dst, so it is assumed to be large enough. The stub is trusted to write only what it decoded.

The vulnerable code

After the wide loops, the stub is left with 1 to 63 characters. It handles them at the label L_finalBit with a single masked 64-byte store. Here are the relevant lines at the parent of the fix commit, which is the same code as Corretto 21.0.13.0.11:

Read it as arithmetic. output_size is (length >> 2) * 3: the number of bytes that the complete four-character groups in the tail will produce. If the tail ends in =, the code at L_padding subtracts one, and if the character before that is also =, it subtracts one more.

Now give it a tail of one, two or three characters. length >> 2 is 0, so output_size starts at 0, and the padding code takes it to -1 or -2. Nobody checks for that.

The output mask is supposed to have output_size low bits set, and it is built with BZHI: “zero the high bits starting at this index”. BZHI reads the index from the low 8 bits of the register. For -1 that is 0xff, for -2 it is 0xfe, and for any index of 64 or more the instruction leaves the source alone. The source is all ones. So the mask that should select zero bytes selects all 64.

There is an error check in between, and it does not help. The stub pre-fills its input register with the character 'a' (0x61616161) so that the unused lanes look like valid Base64, then merges in the real characters under the input mask. The padding code has already shifted the = out of that mask, so what is left is at most one or two real characters and a lot of a. Everything decodes cleanly. evmovdqub then stores the whole 64-byte vector at the current output position.

The array was sized for the real output. For a tail of = that is two bytes more than the full blocks produce, so 62 of the 64 bytes land past the end of the array. The stub returns, Java notices the stray = and throws IllegalArgumentException. The exception is correct and too late.

What exactly gets written

Three things about that 64-byte store decide everything that follows.

First, the size is what the arithmetic predicts: 62 bytes past the end of the array for a tail of =, X= or XY=, and 63 for X==. A tail of == or === writes nothing extra.

Second, the position scales with the input. With 126 full 64-character blocks in front of a one-character tail, the store lands at index 6050 to 6111 of what would have been a byte[6050]. The attacker picks the size of the buffer by picking the length of the header.

Third, and this decides everything that follows: the bytes are constant. The stub pre-fills its input with 'a', so the vector it stores is the decode of aaaa repeated, 69 a6 9a sixteen times over, except that its last sixteen bytes are all 9a. Only the first two bytes follow the input, and those two are inside the array. Every single out-of-bounds byte is fixed by the stub. An attacker controls where the write lands and when. Not what it says. You can see those exact constant bytes land on a live object in the crash report below.

Finding a door: Jenkins

A library bug needs a host application, and I wanted one that an attacker can reach before authentication, unmodified. Jenkins qualified on the first read of its source. Its security filter chain passes every request that has a Basic header to jenkins.security.BasicHeaderProcessor:

Line 76 at tag jenkins-2.580.2 decodes whatever follows Basic with the basic decoder, into an exactly sized array, before it has looked at a user name. If the decode throws, Jenkins shrugs, treats the credentials as empty and answers 401. From the outside, a trigger request looks like any failed login.

The official Jenkins image was no use for a clean comparison: it bundles Temurin, which had no fixed build when I set the lab up, and I wanted the vulnerable and the fixed JDK from one vendor with nothing else changed. So the lab runs the official Jenkins 2.580.2 war, checksum-pinned, on two Corretto tarballs: 21.0.13.0.11, the last vulnerable build, and 21.0.13.1.2, the first fixed one. Corretto’s source at those two tags differs in the stub file by exactly the four lines of the fix. The command line is java -Djava.awt.headless=true -jar jenkins.war --httpPort=8080. No tuning flags, no diagnostic flags, no debug build.

Jenkins caps request headers at 8 KiB, which allows 126 full blocks before the tail. So the trigger is:

Sent to a freshly started Jenkins, this request does nothing. Jenkins answers 401 and carries on. Two more things have to be true first, and neither is in the advisory.

The trigger that disarms itself

The first is the detail from earlier: the stub only exists where decode0 is C2-compiled, and a freshly started Jenkins has never decoded anything. So the PoC first sends well-formed Basic headers, about 16,000 of them, small HEAD / requests whose value decodes to AAAAAA with no colon in it, so no account is ever looked up. With --jit-state the PoC reads the compiler’s own view of the method from inside the lab container between phases. That is lab instrumentation, not part of the attack, and it is where the second problem shows up:

After the well-formed warm-up, decode0 is at tier 4 and in use. Then one malformed value arrives, a harmless 9-character one, and the tier 4 code is marked “not entrant”. The compiled decode0 has never seen the branch that throws, so HotSpot deoptimizes the method and sends it back to the interpreter. And the interpreter does not use the stub.

In other words: warm the JVM up with valid input, send the trigger, and the first trigger may hit the stub, but it also switches the stub off for every request after it. The bug protects itself for a while. To get past that, the PoC runs a second warm-up of about 12,000 short malformed values. They are below the 32-character threshold of the vector path, so they are harmless, but they make decode0 throw from the same branch the trigger will use, until C2 compiles it again with that branch included. The last line above shows the new tier 4 version in use. Now the stub stays armed.

And even then, a trigger request sent on its own gets a 401 from a JVM that stays perfectly healthy.

One at a time, nothing happens

With the JIT in the right state the write happens on every trigger request. It just does not hit anything.

HotSpot gives every thread a thread-local allocation buffer, a TLAB: a private slice of the young generation where the thread allocates by bumping a pointer. The decode buffer for the trigger is a byte[6050], an object of 6072 bytes: 16 bytes of header, the data, 6 bytes of padding. The stub’s store covers the last 8 bytes of that object and the 56 bytes after it. Inside a TLAB, the memory after the newest object is simply unused. The overrun scribbles on empty space, and the next allocation overwrites it.

For damage, the buffer has to be allocated outside the TLAB, in the shared part of the young generation, and another thread has to allocate its own object directly behind it before the store happens. A 6 KB array often does not fit in what is left of a thread’s TLAB, and when the leftover is too large to throw away, HotSpot allocates the array directly in the shared young generation, where the next allocation by any other thread lands right behind it. That part of the explanation comes from reading the HotSpot source and from the crash frames below; I did not trace the allocation decision itself. What I did measure is the consequence: run the PoC with --sequential and it sends the same 5,120 trigger requests one at a time on a single connection, and the warm, vulnerable JVM answers every one with a 401 and never notices. 5,120 overruns into the heap, and it does not die.

So the requests have to be decoded at the same moment. My early attempts sent the trigger as ordinary pipelined traffic. They did crash the target, but only after many more requests, and far fewer with a 1 GiB container memory limit than without. Those were scratch trials that I did not keep as evidence, so take them as history and not as a result. They are where the lab’s 1 GiB limit comes from: with it, HotSpot picks the Serial collector and a 256 MB heap by itself. The final PoC does something more deliberate: each round opens 128 connections, sends each request except its last two bytes, waits, and then releases all 128 final CRLFs together. In the captured run they arrive within 2.4 ms of each other. The same JVM that had just shrugged off 5,120 sequential triggers dies in the first round once the requests land together.

The crash

Here is the JVM’s own account of the captured run, from evidence/target-vuln-hs_err.log. Nothing in it was produced by the PoC; the script only copies the file out of the stopped container.

Read it from the bottom up.

Narrow klass base is where this JVM’s compressed class pointers start. Every Java object has a header: an 8-byte mark word, then a 4-byte compressed class pointer, which the JVM turns into a real address by adding that base. The object right behind the decode buffer received the stub’s vector over its header: mark word 9a 69 a6 9a 69 a6 9a 69, class pointer a6 9a 69 a6. As a little-endian integer that class pointer is 0xa6699aa6.

RAX is 0x00007407e5699aa6. That is the narrow klass base, 0x000074073f000000, plus 0xa6699aa6. The JVM took four bytes of Base64 decoder output, believed they were a class, and went looking for it. si_addr is RAX + 0xc, and nothing is mapped there.

The stack says who was looking. The crashing thread is named Handling GET / from 172.17.0.1: it is one of my own requests, inside BasicHeaderProcessor.doFilter, lower-casing its own 8 KB header. It asked the allocator for a fresh array, another request’s decode ran over that array’s header a moment later, and when the allocation slow path came back to finish its bookkeeping, the class was gone. The attack traffic corrupted the attack traffic.

From the attacker’s side, the same moment looks like this (evidence/poc-vuln.txt):

Exit code 134 is the JVM’s own abort, and oom_killed=false rules out the container limit. In the capture, the 128 CRLFs arrive between 07:38:48.231776 and 07:38:48.234166, and the target sends its first RST at 07:38:48.371985. Jenkins was gone about 140 milliseconds after the burst.

The write only does damage when a live object happens to sit behind one of the 128 decode buffers, and the JIT has to have finished recompiling decode0, which cannot be seen from the network. So a round can miss; in the captured run the JVM died in the first round. The crashing frame also differs from run to run, because it is whichever thread first touches a smashed header. What stays constant is the faulting class pointer: the same narrow-klass-base + 0xa6699aa6 sum every time.

Negative control

Same script, same Jenkins war, Corretto 21.0.13.1.2. The JIT goes through the same states, so the fixed stub is reached just like the vulnerable one (evidence/poc-fixed.txt):

5,120 trigger requests, 5,120 polite 401s.

What this is, and what it is not

What I can prove is unauthenticated corruption of the Java heap of a real, unmodified product over the network, ending in a JVM crash. That is a remote crash of Jenkins with zero credentials, and it shows the out-of-bounds write landing on live objects of a real product with stock JVM flags.

It is not what the advisory rates. Oracle says takeover, and the reporter describes code execution and heap disclosure. I did not build an exploit chain against Jenkins. I read the saved crash reports against the HotSpot source to see what an attacker would be working with. The short version:

The primitive is a constant write. The object behind the decode buffer always receives the same mark word, the same class pointer 0xa6699aa6 and, in the next four bytes, 0x9aa6699a: an array’s length, or an object’s first field. The attacker chooses the size of the buffer, the timing, and what the neighbouring requests allocate. None of the bytes.

For reading memory, the interesting part is that length. 0x9aa6699a is negative as a Java int, but HotSpot compares array indexes unsigned, so an array with that length would accept any index. In Jenkins’ Basic header path, though, the code that consumes these arrays reads the length as a signed number first and bails out with a NegativeArraySizeException. No response in any of my runs carried heap bytes.

For control flow, the class pointer is the one pointer in an object header that leads to code. Every victim gets the same one, and in every saved report its target was unmapped memory. Turning that into something useful would need attacker-chosen content at that fixed address, or a victim object that survives without its class being consulted. The JVM gives a corrupted object very little time: about 140 ms in the captured run.

None of this says the disclosed impact is out of reach. It says where I stopped against Jenkins. The next section is what happened when I took the network out of the picture and kept going.

Beyond the crash: command execution in the lab

Added on 2026-11-18, after this post first went up. Everything in this section happens inside a test JVM in the lab. Nothing in it was sent to Jenkins.

That analysis left one door open: a corrupted object is only useful if it survives without its class being consulted. So I asked a narrower question. Given this exact overflow on this exact build, can the corruption be carried all the way to running a command? I wrote a small harness, poc/CmdExecProbe.java, that runs in a throwaway JVM inside the vulnerable lab image and triggers the real stub with 64 A characters and one =. It allocates five objects back to back: the decode buffer, two 48-byte arrays, and two tiny objects of different classes, Normal and Altered, that implement the same one-method interface. Then five things happen.

One: the overflow. The store runs over the header of the first array. Its class pointer is garbage and its length reads 0x9aa6699a, the constant from the analysis above. A plain byte store into this array kills the JVM, because the bastore bytecode looks at the class first. An earlier probe of mine died exactly there.

Two: a second, cleaner primitive. C2-compiled System.arraycopy does not look at the class, and HotSpot compares indexes unsigned, so that “negative” length admits any index. One 4-byte copy through the smashed array raises the length field of the second array from 48 to 256. The second array keeps a valid byte[] header, so ordinary bytecode can read and write past its real end.

Three: type confusion. Through the inflated array the harness reads the compressed class pointer of the Altered object and writes those four bytes over the class pointer of the Normal object next to it.

Four: controlled dispatch. The harness calls the one interface method on the Normal object. Before the overwrite the call returns NORMAL. After it, the same call on the same reference runs the method of Altered: invokeinterface looks up the receiver’s class when it runs, and that class is now whatever those four bytes say.

Five: command execution. The method of Altered calls Runtime.getRuntime().exec("/usr/bin/id") and returns what the command printed (evidence/impact-cmdexec-vuln.txt):

victim.length = -1700370022 is 0x9aa6699a read as a signed int: the stub’s bytes again. 08cc1401 and 00281501 are the two compressed class pointers in memory order. Steps [3] and [5] are the same line of Java on the same object; all that changed in between is four bytes, written at index 56 to 59 of an array whose real length is 48. And uid=1000(jenkins) is id running as the user of the lab container.

A second run with -XX:-UseTLAB, which puts every allocation into the shared part of the young generation where the network PoC’s decode buffer does its damage, printed the same result, and both JVMs exited normally. On the fixed build the harness tries 20 times and gives up (evidence/impact-cmdexec-fixed.txt):

Now the part that matters more than the output. This is not remote code execution against Jenkins, and I do not want it read that way.

It is in-process. One single-threaded JVM, with a 4 GB heap so that no garbage collection interferes, puts its own objects next to each other and reads the class pointers it needs from its own neighbours. Over the network an attacker gets adjacency only by chance among concurrent requests, and needs an information leak to learn the class pointer to write.

And it ends in a stand-in gadget. The corruption genuinely redirects the call. But the method the call lands in, the one with Runtime.exec in it, I wrote myself, and the harness even calls it directly while warming up. So id running is not the proof; the same call returning NORMAL before the overwrite and the command output after it is. A remote attacker can only redirect to a class the target JVM has already loaded, and I did not search for one that does something useful when called on the wrong object.

What the harness shows is narrower than the advisory and still worth knowing: the bug is a code-execution primitive, not only a way to crash a JVM. Between this and a remote attack on Jenkins lies the per-application work: grooming a multi-threaded heap through HTTP requests, a leak, and a gadget that is already loaded. I have not built that.

The claims, in one table

ClaimStatusEvidence
An unauthenticated HTTP request reaches the vulnerable decode in unmodified Jenkins 2.580.2Provenevidence/target-vuln-hs_err.log, capture/exploit.pcap
The PoC corrupts the heap of the real product and crashes the JVM, pre-auth, default JVM flagsConfirmed (negative control on Corretto 21.0.13.1.2)evidence/poc-vuln.txt, evidence/poc-fixed.txt
The corruption is the stub’s constant store: the faulting class pointer is narrow klass base + 0xa6699aa6Provenevidence/target-vuln-hs_err.log

Heap memory disclosureNot reachedthe smashed length is read signed by Jenkins’ consumers and throws; no response carried heap bytes
In a separate in-lab harness on the same vulnerable build, the overflow is driven to controlled method dispatch: a C2 arraycopy write inflates an adjacent array’s length (a secondary read/write primitive whose own class stays valid), an out-of-bounds bastore overwrites a neighbouring object’s compressed class pointer, and an invokeinterface call is redirected to a different classProven (in-process harness; negative control clean on Corretto 21.0.13.1.2)evidence/impact-cmdexec-vuln.txt, evidence/impact-cmdexec-fixed.txt, poc/CmdExecProbe.java
That redirected dispatch reaches a Runtime.exec() sink and runs a benign command (/usr/bin/id), returning its output: the bug is a code-execution primitive, not DoS-onlyProven (in-process; stand-in gadget, the exec sink is attacker-authored)evidence/impact-cmdexec-vuln.txt
Remote code execution against Jenkins over the networkNot reachedthe in-process chain is not interleaved with multi-threaded heap grooming, a class-pointer info leak and an already-loaded gadget class

I tested one product, one JDK line, one AMD CPU, plain HTTP with no reverse proxy, and a Jenkins in its first-boot state. Jenkins’ Basic header filter sits in the same place before and after setup, but a busy, configured instance allocates differently, and a proxy that buffers whole requests would release them on its own schedule. I have not tested either.

Detection

The repository has one Suricata rule, and it is experimental / minimally validated: it was tested only against the attack capture from this lab. I make no claim about coverage or false positives beyond that.

It matches an Authorization: Basic value made of one or more full 64-character blocks followed by a short padded tail. On the attack capture it fired 128 times, once per trigger request, and stayed quiet on the roughly 2,000 warm-up requests in the same file.

Its limits are real. It looks only at the Basic header, while the bug is reachable through any field a Java service decodes with java.util.Base64. It needs plaintext HTTP or TLS inspection. Its expression also admits a four-character tail, which is not a trigger. And there is no log-based rule, because I found nothing to key on: Jenkins handles the decoder’s exception the way it handles any malformed header, and the JVM’s fatal error report only exists once the attack has already worked. Details are in detection/README.md.

The fix

JDK-8393212, “Base64 optimization improvements”, adds two instructions and a comment:

If fewer than four characters remain, the stub now jumps to L_bruteForce, its scalar path, which decodes complete groups only and leaves the rest to Java. That is the right place to cut. A tail shorter than four characters cannot contain a complete group, so there is nothing for the vector code to do with it, and output_size can no longer go below zero. The jdk21u change is commit 8e115fb5c7c5, and the same change went into jdk17u, jdk25u and jdk27u. The fixed OpenJDK versions are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.

If you cannot upgrade today, either -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics or -XX:UseAVX=2 removes the vulnerable path. The first costs you the fast Base64 decoder. The second costs you AVX-512 across the whole JVM.

Advisory and fix

Advisory: Oracle Critical Patch Update Advisory, November 2026.

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post from the repository. You need Docker on an x86-64 Linux host whose CPU has AVX-512 VBMI; setup.py checks for it and refuses to continue otherwise.

The raw output of every run quoted here, the capture and the rule are in the repository: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-114938.

entry.title: CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell): HotSpot AVX-512 Base64 Heap Overflow -- Crashing Jenkins Before Login

entry.content:
The advisory

nginx is one of the most widely deployed web servers and reverse proxies, and HTTP/2 over TLS is a common way to run it. On 2026-11-18 nginx.org published “Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control”, CVE-2026-123007, for every release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. The advisory’s own words for the impact are “segmentation fault in a worker process, or might have potential other impact”. The bug has also been described publicly as leading to remote code execution, and it carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2.

I set out to reproduce it on stock nginx and see how far the advisory’s sentence could be turned into something observable. What I can show is the first half: one unauthenticated HTTP/2 connection kills a worker process of nginx 1.30.6 from the official image with SIGSEGV, and an AddressSanitizer build of the same commit names the call that does it, a memcpy in the TLS send path whose length is 0x80000000243e3ffa. I did not attempt code execution, so that part stays “not reached”. nginx 1.30.7 refuses the attack at its first step.

The catch is the price. The crash costs 4,294,967,300 WINDOW_UPDATE frames, about 60 GiB of traffic on a single connection, and most of this post is about why nginx makes it that expensive.

PoC, live capture, evidence and detection rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-123007

How nginx does HTTP/2 flow control

HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests (“streams”) over one TCP connection. To stop a fast sender from flooding a slow receiver, the protocol has credit-based flow control. Every stream has a send window and the connection as a whole has one too. A sender may only emit DATA while both windows are positive, and each DATA frame is subtracted from both. The receiver hands credit back with WINDOW_UPDATE frames, one per stream or for the connection (stream 0).

Two rules of the protocol matter here. A window may never exceed 2^31-1; a WINDOW_UPDATE that would push it higher is a flow-control error and the connection must be closed. And any stream can be cancelled by the client at any time with RST_STREAM.

In nginx the connection window lives in h2c->send_window, and the limit is NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW. A response body reaches the client in three steps. The HTTP/2 filter, ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), cuts it into DATA frames and puts them on the connection’s output queue. ngx_http_v2_send_output_queue() hands the queue to the transport. On a TLS connection the transport is ngx_ssl_send_chain(), which copies the frames into a 16 KiB buffer on their way to being encrypted.

The detail that makes this bug possible is the moment at which nginx does the bookkeeping. The window is debited when a DATA frame is queued, not when it is written to the socket. Normally the difference is invisible, because nginx writes queued frames at once whenever the socket is writable. It only shows if the socket is full: then frames sit in the queue, already paid for, but not yet sent.

The vulnerable code

I started from the fix commit, b89c4100 (“HTTP/2: account for queued frames when validating WINDOW_UPDATE”), and read the 1.30.6 sources backwards from it to the frames that reach the code, and forwards to wherever the bad value ends up. Three statements in three functions are the whole root cause. These are the statements that matter, lifted out of their functions:

Each one is reasonable alone. Together they count the same bytes twice. Suppose 8 MB of DATA sits in the queue. The window has already been debited by 8 MB, so the check in the middle will let the client send a WINDOW_UPDATE for those 8 MB: as far as the check can tell, the window has room. Now the client cancels the streams. The cleanup handler sees 8 MB of frames that will never be sent and, correctly, gives the window back what was debited for them. The client has been credited once by its own WINDOW_UPDATE and once by the refund. The window is now above 2^31-1, a state the code assumes cannot exist.

What happens next is the part I like. send_window is a size_t. Once it is larger than NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW, the subtraction on the right-hand side of the check wraps around to an enormous unsigned number, and no increment is ever greater than that. The one guard on the window has switched itself off. Every further WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted, and the window can be grown to any 64-bit value.

The sink is two files away:

When nginx builds the next DATA frame it compares the amount it wants to send with the window, cast to a signed off_t. A window of 2^63 or more is negative as an off_t, so the limit becomes negative, ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow() builds a buffer whose last pointer is pos plus a negative number, and ngx_ssl_send_chain() computes a negative size. There are two clamps on size before the copy, but both only cap it from above. A negative value passes them and arrives at memcpy as a length of about 2^63.

The trigger

On paper the recipe is short: queue some DATA, send a WINDOW_UPDATE for it, cancel the streams, then inflate the window and ask for one more frame. The preconditions are equally short. HTTP/2 must be enabled, and for the memcpy sink shown here the connection must be TLS. No authentication is involved, and every frame is an ordinary one that a normal client sends all day.

In practice nginx has four mechanisms that get in the way, none of them written for this bug. I found them one at a time while building the PoC.

The queue empties itself. nginx writes queued frames as soon as the socket accepts them, so the frames have to be held in the queue while WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM are processed. The way to do that is to fill the TCP path: open the window of one stream, the “plug”, and stop reading. nginx writes until the kernel buffers on both sides are full and then blocks. Everything it queues after that stays queued.

Only whole, untouched frames are refunded. A frame that has been partly written is marked blocked and is not refunded on cancellation. And one stream can only queue what one send_chain call produces, 65536 bytes with the default output_buffers 2 32k. So the refund has to come from many streams: 127 of them, 8323072 bytes, and that has to be more than what the TCP path swallowed for the plug.

The flood guard. nginx closes an HTTP/2 connection when total_bytes / 8 > payload_bytes + 1048576. WINDOW_UPDATE frames are not payload. By that formula a connection that carries nothing but control frames is cut off after about 8 MiB, so one eighth of the whole exchange has to be DATA from the server.

The idle guard. With no stream open, nginx counts every read on the connection and closes it after ten times keepalive_requests. My first attempt at the flood died here, with http2 flood detected in the info log. One request has to stay open the whole time.

Walking the attack

The script, poc.py, does it in three stages on one connection.

Stage 1: overflow

It sends SETTINGS with INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE=0, so no stream can send any DATA, and a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that takes the connection window from its initial 65535 to exactly 2^31-1. Then it sends 128 GET requests for a static file, the default limit for concurrent streams. nginx answers all of them with headers and no body.

Next it gives stream 255, the plug, a window of 6 MiB and stops reading from the socket. nginx starts sending and blocks in write. Now comes one burst, small enough to travel in a single packet: 127 stream WINDOW_UPDATEs of 65536 bytes, a connection WINDOW_UPDATE for the same 8323072 bytes, and 128 RST_STREAM frames.

nginx processes them in order. For each of the 127 streams it builds 65536 bytes of DATA, queues them behind the blocked write and debits the window. It accepts the connection WINDOW_UPDATE, because the debit made room for it. Then it handles the cancellations and refunds everything that is still queued.

The script cannot read nginx’s memory, but it does not have to. The window is fully determined by what the client sent and received: the initial window, plus every credit it sent, minus every DATA byte that actually arrived, because every byte that did not arrive was refunded. After the burst it drains the socket and counts 4243456 bytes on the plug stream and nothing on the others. That puts the window at 2147483647 + 8323072 - 4243456 = 2151563263, which is 4079616 above the limit.

To prove it without crashing anything, the script sends one WINDOW_UPDATE of 2^31-1. A correct server must answer that with GOAWAY. This one answers the PING that follows.

Stage 2: grow

From here the window only needs to get big. Each WINDOW_UPDATE adds at most 2^31-1, so reaching 2^63 takes 2^32 of them. I looked for a shortcut and did not find one: every increase is a 13-byte frame worth at most 2^31-1, and the refund path is net zero. 2^32 frames of 13 bytes is 52.0 GiB.

The flood guard turns that into a download job as well. One eighth of the exchange has to be payload, which is 7.4 GiB of response DATA. Request bodies do not help with a static file, because nginx discards them without counting. And keepalive_requests caps a connection at 1000 requests, of which stage 1 already used 128. That is why the lab serves a 64 MiB file: 119 downloads of it fit in the budget. A site that only has small responses was not tested, and I expect it to stop the attack at the flood guard.

So stage 2 is a loop: send a batch of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, 1260 to a TLS record, keep one download running, read what comes back, and never let the ratio slip. On loopback it takes 41 seconds.

Stage 3: trigger

The window is now 2^63 plus a little. The script opens one more stream, checks with a PING that the connection is healthy, and gives that stream a window of 16384 bytes. nginx goes to build a single DATA frame.

The crash

This is the run that ships in the repository, against the stock binary, from evidence/poc-vuln.txt. I have cut the progress lines of stage 2:

The line to look at is “0 of 8323072 bytes on the cancelled streams”. Those bytes were credited and never delivered. The numbers close, too: the final window is the 2151563263 from stage 1, plus 4294967301 increments of 2^31-1 (the probe and the flood), minus the 7985954816 bytes of the 119 completed downloads.

A dropped connection is not proof of a crash by itself, so here is the server’s side of the same second, from evidence/target-vuln.txt:

Signal 11, on a binary I did not build. But a signal is not a location. I wanted the backtrace, and the lab host pipes core dumps to apport, which throws away cores from containers. Instead of fighting that, I rebuilt the same commit (fb0e979c, the 1.30.6 release tag) with AddressSanitizer and the same configure modules as the package, and ran the same script against it. From evidence/target-vuln-asan.txt:

Read it from the bottom of the stack. Frame 23 is the WINDOW_UPDATE handler: the trigger frame arrived and woke the stream. Frame 4 is ngx_http_v2_send_chain() building the DATA frame. Frame 1 is ngx_ssl_send_chain() at line 3117, the copy into the TLS buffer.

The report type looks odd for an overflow. AddressSanitizer checks the arguments of memcpy before it lets the copy run, and with a length this size the first thing it notices is that source and destination overlap. Subtract the ends of either range and you get 0x80000000243e3ffa, exactly the window the script printed. The destination starts 9 bytes into a 16384-byte heap region allocated in ngx_ssl_send_chain() at line 3074, the TLS buffer. Nine bytes is the size of an HTTP/2 frame header, presumably the one for this DATA frame. The source is a 32768-byte file buffer.

Two limits of this proof are worth stating. AddressSanitizer stops the call before a single byte is copied, so the report shows the arguments, not what gets overwritten. And on the stock build I have the signal but no backtrace, so “the SIGSEGV is inside this memcpy” rests on the sanitizer build of the same commit, not on a core dump of the stock one.

Negative control

The same script, unchanged, against nginx 1.30.7 from the official image (evidence/poc-patched.txt):

And the patched server says why, in evidence/target-patched.txt:

The whole run takes about two seconds and no worker exits. The fix stops the attack at the first frame that matters.

Impact

What I demonstrated is an unauthenticated remote crash of one nginx worker. The worker that owns the attack connection dies, and the master starts a replacement within the same second. One run takes about 45 seconds and 60 GiB on loopback. I did not try to keep all workers down, so I make no claim about a sustained outage.

In this lab the result was deterministic. Every run that reached stage 3 crashed the worker: four on the stock build and two on the sanitizer build, and 1.30.7 refused all four attempts. The one way I know to make it fail is a network path that buffers more than the 8323072 bytes of stage 1. Docker’s own port publishing does that, as does an ssh tunnel: the queued frames get sent, the refund never happens, and the script notices and stops. That is why the lab containers share the host’s network namespace and why the script runs on the lab host. It also means that a buffering proxy in front of nginx breaks this PoC as written. I would not read that as a mitigation.

ClaimStatusEvidence

“Not reached” means what it says. The value that reaches memcpy here is 2^63 plus a remainder, because the sign bit is all a crash needs. I did not explore what other values would do.

Detection

The attack is HTTP/2 inside TLS 1.3. A network sensor that does not terminate TLS sees no frames at all, only one long-lived connection that carries about 52 GiB from client to server against 7.4 GiB the other way. I wrote no network rule: a Suricata rule could not be validated against an encrypted capture, and a volume heuristic would not be specific to this bug.

What nginx logs is more useful. The repository has two Sigma rules for the error log, both experimental / minimally validated. Each was tested only against the log of my one attack run and against one benign sample, nginx 1.30.7 starting up and serving normal HTTP/2 requests. Nobody has measured their false-positive rate.

  • cve-2026-123007-crash.yml matches worker process N exited on signal 11. It works at the stock log level, and it fires on any worker SIGSEGV, whatever the cause. A worker dying on signal 11 deserves a look in any case.
  • cve-2026-123007-stream-cancel.yml matches client canceled stream. Stage 1 leaves 128 of these on one connection within one second. It needs error_log at info, which is not the default, and a threshold in the SIEM (50 or more in 60 seconds) to be of any use, because single cancellations are normal traffic.

The rules and their limits are in detection/.

The fix

Commit b89c4100, “HTTP/2: account for queued frames when validating WINDOW_UPDATE”, adds a counter to the connection, h2c->send_queued, for the bytes in DATA frames that are queued but not yet sent. The bound in the WINDOW_UPDATE handler becomes:

This goes to the cause and not the symptom. The window is still debited at queue time and still refunded on cancellation, but the client can no longer be credited for bytes that are only queued, so credit and refund cannot both land for the same bytes. The log line from the negative control is consistent with that. The window it reports, 2143248383, is 4235264 below the limit, about what the script saw arrive on the plug stream (4227072 bytes); the 8323072 queued bytes no longer make room for a WINDOW_UPDATE.

Affected: nginx 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. Fixed: 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline). If HTTP/2 is enabled, upgrade.

Advisory and fix

2026-11-18nginx.org publishes “Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control” (CVE-2026-123007, reported by Xint.io); fixed in nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9
2026-11-18Reproduction and this write-up

References: nginx security advisories, F5 article K000163926, fix commit b89c4100.

Reproduction

Everything above can be checked from the repository. You need a Linux x86_64 host with Docker and Python 3; the scripts use only the standard library. Run poc.py on the Docker host itself, since stage 1 needs a direct TCP connection to nginx.

The capture in the repository is partial by design, since nobody wants a 60 GiB pcap: the first 700 packets with a TLS key log that decrypts them, which covers all of stage 1, and every SYN, FIN and RST of the run. The full evidence, the capture and the rules are at al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-123007.

entry.content:
The advisory

The Document Foundation published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104007 on November 16, 2026. The advisory describes code execution through JDBC driver loading when a user opens a crafted document. CVSS 4.0: 8.5 High. Affected: LibreOffice 26.2 through 26.2.6 and 26.8 through 26.8.1. The fix shipped in 26.2.7 and 26.8.2.

The advisory is sparse on details, but the CWE (CWE-829, Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere) and the mention of JDBC drivers told me where to look. There is a related CVE – CVE-2026-63277 – that describes the same underlying problem (remote code execution through JDBC driver loading) but via a different route: calcext:data-mappings and an SQL provider. That one was fixed in 26.2.5. CVE-2026-104007 is a new route to the same driver-loading code, through pivot tables. No public proof of concept existed for this route.

I built a full attack chain from a crafted ODS spreadsheet to arbitrary Java code execution inside the LibreOffice JVM, confirmed it on 26.2.6.3, and verified the fix blocks it on 26.2.7.2.

PoC, detection rules, and live pcap: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-104007

How LibreOffice loads JDBC drivers

LibreOffice can connect to databases through Java JDBC drivers. The connection settings live in ODB files – OpenDocument Database documents – which are ZIP archives containing XML metadata. Among other things, an ODB’s db:driver-settings element names the JDBC driver class and the classpath to load it from:

In normal use, the driver classpath comes from the user’s own LibreOffice JDBC driver configuration, which the user sets up manually. The ODB file is trusted because the user created it. But what happens when LibreOffice opens an ODB it did not create, one that specifies a classpath the user never configured?

Before 26.2.7, LibreOffice uses the classpath from the ODB itself. It loads the named Java class from the path the ODB specifies, and if that class has a static initializer, it runs in the LibreOffice JVM process. The document controls what code the application loads.

The pivot table route

LibreOffice spreadsheets (ODS files) support pivot tables, which LibreOffice calls “data pilots.” A pivot table can be backed by a database source, specified in the ODS content XML:

The key detail: table:database-name can be a URL. When the pivot table refreshes, LibreOffice resolves that URL and fetches the ODB. In affected versions, this fetch happens without a link-update consent dialog. The user opens the spreadsheet, the pivot table tries to refresh, and LibreOffice silently downloads the ODB from wherever the attacker pointed it.

This is the route CVE-2026-104007 takes. The related CVE-2026-63277 reached the same driver-loading code through calcext:data-mappings and was fixed in 26.2.5, but the pivot table path remained open until 26.2.7.

The attack chain

The chain has five links. I built each one:

  1. Crafted ODS. A minimal ODS spreadsheet with a pivot table whose table:database-source-sql element names an HTTP URL as the database. The spreadsheet does nothing else – no macros, no other active content. The pivot table is the entire attack surface.

  2. HTTP-served ODB. A Python HTTP server on loopback port 9007 serves poc.odb. When LibreOffice opens the ODS and refreshes the pivot table, it reaches out to this URL. The ODB is a minimal database document specifying db:java-driver-class="MaliciousDriver" and db:java-classpath="file:///work/malicious-driver.jar".

  3. Malicious JAR. A compiled Java class implementing java.sql.Driver. The static initializer runs id, hostname, and uname -a, writing the output to /tmp/pwned.txt. Nothing destructive – just enough to prove the code ran and to identify the execution context.

  4. Pivot table refresh. In the lab, the PoC opens the ODS via LibreOffice’s UNO API and calls DataPilotTable.refresh(). In a real attack, the refresh would happen when the user interacts with the pivot table or through an embedded macro.

  5. Driver loads, code executes. LibreOffice fetches the ODB, reads the driver settings, and loads MaliciousDriver from the attacker-specified classpath. The static initializer fires. The marker file appears.

One limitation: after the CVE-2026-63277 fix in 26.2.5, the classpath is restricted to file:// URLs. The JAR cannot be fetched over HTTP; it must already exist on the target filesystem. An attacker would deliver it by another means – an email attachment, a download, a shared drive – or target a known path. This restriction narrows the attack but does not prevent it.

The proof

On LibreOffice 26.2.6.3, the PoC runs the full chain. The pivot table refreshes, LibreOffice fetches the ODB, and the malicious driver executes:

The marker file /tmp/pwned.txt written by the malicious driver inside the container:

The pcap from the vulnerable container (capture/vuln-capture.pcap, 12242 bytes, 70 packets) shows LibreOffice reaching out over HTTP:

LibreOffice issues multiple requests – OPTIONS, then HEAD, then GET – to retrieve the ODB. The User-Agent header confirms the vulnerable version.

Negative control

The same PoC against LibreOffice 26.2.7.2:

No marker file. The pcap from the patched container is 24 bytes – the file header only, zero packets. LibreOffice 26.2.7.2 did not make any HTTP request. The fix blocks the ODB fetch before the driver-loading code is ever reached.

Impact

The attack achieves arbitrary code execution in the LibreOffice JVM process when a user opens a crafted spreadsheet, with two preconditions: Java must be enabled in LibreOffice, and the malicious JAR must be on the target filesystem.

The pivot table route is distinct from CVE-2026-63277’s calcext:data-mappings route. Even installations that applied the 26.2.5 fix for CVE-2026-63277 remained vulnerable through CVE-2026-104007 until 26.2.7.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Code execution on LibreOffice 26.2.6.3Provenevidence/poc-vuln-pwned.txt, evidence/poc-console-output.txt
Full attack chain from crafted ODS to code executionProvenevidence/poc-console-output.txt, capture/vuln-capture.pcap
Patched version unaffectedConfirmedevidence/poc-console-output.txt, evidence/capture-patched.pcap
Code execution without pre-staged JARNot reachedCVE-2026-63277 fix restricts classpath to file:// only

Detection

The repository includes experimental detection rules for the network and file indicators of this attack. These are research artifacts, not production-grade signatures. Each was tested against the exploit capture or sample and one benign fixture only.

Suricata (detection/cve-2026-104007.rules): two rules detecting (1) HTTP responses delivering ODB files via Content-Type application/vnd.sun.xml.base, and (2) LibreOffice User-Agent requesting a .odb URI. Both require plaintext HTTP inspection.

YARA (detection/cve-2026-104007.yar): two rules matching (1) ODS files containing a pivot table with an HTTP-referenced database source, and (2) ODB files specifying both a JDBC driver class and a classpath. Useful at email gateways or endpoint scanners.

Both rule sets fired on the exploit samples and stayed silent on the benign fixtures. See detection/README.md for full test results and limitations.

The fix

The fix in 26.2.7 / 26.8.2 applies two restrictions. First, the JDBC driver location is sourced exclusively from the user’s own configured drivers, ignoring any classpath specified in the database document. Second, pivot tables whose data source names a URL-based database document require the user to approve link updates before connecting – the unconsented fetch is gone.

The dual fix is important. Restricting the classpath alone would still allow the silent ODB fetch, which is an information-disclosure risk (the attacker learns whether the user opened the document). Requiring consent for link updates is the defense-in-depth layer that blocks the entire chain at its first step.

DateEvent
2026-11-16Advisory published; 26.2.7 and 26.8.2 released
2026-11-17Reproduction confirmed

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post by running three commands from a fresh clone.

The setup requires Docker with access to a Linux x86_64 host. The PoC stages all payload files, runs the exploit, and reports the result with evidence collection.

Full details: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-104007
