entry.content:
The advisory

The Document Foundation published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104692 on November 16, 2026. The advisory describes code execution: a crafted document can call arbitrary Java methods from SQL through LibreOffice’s bundled HSQLDB database engine. CVSS 4.0: 8.5 High. Affected: LibreOffice 26.2 through 26.2.6 and 26.8 through 26.8.1. Fixed in 26.2.7 and 26.8.2.

The advisory is concise. It names the HSQLDB JDBC driver path as the attack vector and credits two independent sets of finders: Thomas Rinsma and Edoardo Geraci at Codean Labs, and Minseong Kim at NSHC Red Alert Labs. No public proof of concept exists. The related CVE-2022-41853 covers the upstream HSQLDB Java-method-call mechanism, and CVE-2007-4575 is the historical LibreOffice/OpenOffice predecessor. Neither has a LibreOffice-specific PoC for this particular JDBC driver bypass.

I built a 1709-byte .odb file that calls three distinct Java methods when opened, confirmed it on LibreOffice 26.2.6.3, and verified the fix blocks it on 26.2.7.3. This is the first public PoC for CVE-2026-104692.

PoC, detection rules, and the crafted document: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-104692

HSQLDB and LibreOffice: a database inside a document

LibreOffice Base stores databases in .odb files, which are ZIP archives following the OpenDocument format. When a user opens an .odb document, LibreOffice connects to the database inside it. For many years, the default embedded database engine has been HSQLDB, bundled as a Java jar file inside the LibreOffice installation.

HSQLDB has a feature that sets it apart from most embedded databases: SQL statements can call arbitrary Java static methods. The CREATE ALIAS statement maps a SQL function name to a fully qualified Java method. After the alias is created, CALL alias(args) invokes the Java method with the given arguments, and the return value comes back as a SQL result. This is not a bug in HSQLDB – it is a documented feature. The same mechanism was the subject of CVE-2022-41853 in upstream HSQLDB (fixed in hsqldb 2.7.1), because it allows untrusted SQL to execute arbitrary code in the JVM.

The critical detail is how the database initializes. When HSQLDB opens a file-based database, it reads db.script – a plain text file containing DDL and DML statements that reconstruct the database schema and data from scratch. Everything in the script runs. If the script contains CREATE ALIAS and CALL statements that point at Java system methods, those methods execute before the user has seen any content. No macros are involved. No security dialog appears.

Inside a .odb file, database/db.script is just another ZIP member. An attacker who controls the .odb controls the script, and the script controls what Java code runs in LibreOffice’s JVM.

Two paths to the same code

LibreOffice connects to its bundled HSQLDB through two paths:

  1. The embedded path. LibreOffice’s internal HSQLDB driver (connectivity/source/drivers/hsqldb/HDriver.cxx) manages the connection. This path applies a class allowlist to restrict which Java methods CREATE ALIAS can reference. The allowlist has been in place for years and blocks dangerous methods such as Runtime.exec.

  2. The JDBC path. LibreOffice’s generic JDBC driver opens the same HSQLDB database with a standard JDBC connection string: jdbc:hsqldb:file:<path>. On this path, the HSQLDB jar processes the .script file directly. The class allowlist from the embedded driver is never applied, because HSQLDB itself does not enforce one.

Both paths open the same database, run the same .script file, and evaluate the same CREATE ALIAS statements. The difference is what happens when the alias points at a Java method outside the built-in set. On the embedded path, LibreOffice’s driver intercepts the call and refuses it. On the JDBC path, nothing does.

This is the gap CVE-2026-104692 exploits. A crafted .odb configured to use the JDBC path – or one where LibreOffice falls back to it – bypasses the class restriction entirely. The document is small, it looks like any other database document, and it triggers on open.

The malicious script

The payload I used is minimal. The db.script inside the crafted .odb contains five SQL statements:

Three CREATE ALIAS statements map SQL names to Java methods: System.setProperty (mutate JVM state), System.getProperty (read environment), and File.createTempFile (write to disk). Two CALL statements exercise them. The property set and the marker file are observables – they prove the methods executed. System.getProperty is called through interactive queries after the database opens, to read user.name, os.name, os.arch, and java.version.

I initially assumed Runtime.exec would be the natural escalation. It is not – and the reason is interesting. HSQLDB 1.8.x’s CREATE ALIAS ... FOR resolves only Java static methods. Runtime.exec() is an instance method. The static accessor Runtime.getRuntime() returns a Runtime object, but java.lang.Runtime is not Serializable, so HSQLDB’s SQL type system cannot represent the return value. The call fails with “Wrong data type: java.lang.Runtime.” Inline Java (CREATE ALIAS ... AS $$...$$) would make Runtime.exec trivial, but that syntax is HSQLDB 2.x only; LibreOffice bundles 1.8.x.

I scanned the full LibreOffice classpath – 36 jars including BeanShell, Rhino, and the UNO bridge – for public static methods that take SQL-compatible arguments and might wrap command execution. The closest candidate was bsh.Remote.eval(String, String), which connects to a remote BeanShell server rather than evaluating code locally. No static wrapper for Runtime.exec or ProcessBuilder.start exists on the classpath. This is a limitation of HSQLDB 1.8.x’s design, not of the vulnerability mechanism itself.

The three demonstrated calls are sufficient to prove the mechanism. System.setProperty and File.createTempFile show that any public static method with SQL-compatible parameter types executes through the JDBC path without restriction. The impact – file creation, JVM state mutation, information disclosure – is meaningful even without a shell.

The entire .odb is 1709 bytes. That is small enough to embed in a phishing email without triggering size-based heuristics, and small enough that no one would look at it twice.

The exploit in action

I ran the PoC against LibreOffice 26.2.6.3 in a Docker container on the lab server. The PoC generates the crafted .odb, extracts the database files, and connects through the JDBC path using the HSQLDB jar from the target LibreOffice installation – the same jar, the same code path.

The JVM property cve.2026.104692 was set to exploited-via-hsqldb-jdbc. A marker file appeared in /tmp/. The system properties came back: the process runs as root on Linux/amd64 with OpenJDK 21.0.13. The exploit succeeded on 3/3 rounds. It is not a race – the script executes synchronously during database initialization, so it fires every time.

Three things matter here. The property mutation proves write access to JVM state. The file creation proves write access to the filesystem. The property reads prove information disclosure. Together, they demonstrate that the JDBC path places no restriction on what Java methods the SQL can invoke.

The negative control

The same .odb against LibreOffice 26.2.7.3, which ships the patched HSQLDB jar:

HSQLDB refused to initialize. The error from the patched jar:

The patched jar denies CREATE ALIAS for Java methods outside the built-in set. This is the right fix: it closes the gap at the source, in the HSQLDB jar, so the restriction applies regardless of which driver path opened the database. The embedded-path allowlist in HDriver.cxx was correct for its path, but the JDBC path needed the same enforcement, and the only place to put it was in HSQLDB itself.

Impact

The advisory describes “arbitrary Java method calls from SQL,” and that is what this PoC demonstrates – constrained to static methods by HSQLDB 1.8.x’s design. An attacker who can get a victim to open a crafted .odb document achieves arbitrary Java static method invocation inside the LibreOffice process. The three calls I demonstrated – property mutation, file creation, information disclosure – are concrete impacts. The mechanism generalizes to any public static method with SQL-compatible parameter types on the JVM classpath.

OS command execution (Runtime.exec) was explicitly investigated and is not reachable through HSQLDB 1.8.x (see the investigation above and evidence/impact-exec-analysis.txt in the repository). If LibreOffice bundled HSQLDB 2.x, which supports inline Java in CREATE ALIAS, Runtime.exec would be trivial. The static-method constraint limits which methods are callable but does not prevent meaningful impact: file creation on disk and information disclosure are real consequences for a victim who opens a document.

The attack requires user interaction (UI:P): the victim must open the document. No prior authentication or access is required (PR:N). The attack is local (AV:L) – the .odb is delivered as a file, not over a protocol.

LibreOffice is installed on hundreds of millions of desktops and is the default office suite on most Linux distributions. The .odb format is less common than .odt or .ods, but it is a standard document format that email gateways and file-sharing services generally allow through without inspection.

Lab deviations

The PoC connects to HSQLDB through java -cp hsqldb.jar SqlTool rather than through the LibreOffice GUI. This is an automation convenience: the JDBC connection string (jdbc:hsqldb:file:<path>) and the HSQLDB jar are identical to what LibreOffice uses internally. The code path that evaluates CREATE ALIAS and executes Java methods is the same code path. The lab runs in Docker containers on a Linux server rather than on a bare-metal desktop, and user interaction (opening the document) is replaced by extracting the database and connecting programmatically. These deviations affect the delivery mechanism, not the vulnerability itself.

Detection

Status: experimental / minimally validated. Each rule was tested against the attack artifact and one benign sample only. No broad variation or false-positive campaign was performed.

Two YARA rules and one Sigma rule are in the repository:

  • YARA rule 1 (structural triage): matches ODF Base documents with an embedded HSQLDB database. High false-positive risk – every legitimate .odb with HSQLDB fires. Use it as a triage signal for extraction.
  • YARA rule 2 (content match): matches extracted db.script files containing CREATE ALIAS ... FOR "java.*" patterns. Low false-positive risk. Requires the .odb to be decompressed before scanning.
  • Sigma rule (blocked attempt): detects the “Access is denied” error message on patched systems. Low false-positive risk. Requires LibreOffice application logs to be forwarded to a SIEM.

No Suricata rule is provided. This is a file-based attack with no CVE-specific network protocol interaction. The delivery channel (email attachment, download link) is generic.

The fix

The fix patches the HSQLDB jar bundled with LibreOffice. The patched jar restricts SQL to HSQLDB built-in functions regardless of access method. This is the correct approach: rather than adding another check in each driver path, the fix ensures the HSQLDB engine itself refuses dangerous CREATE ALIAS calls. Fix developer: Caolan McNamara (Collabora Productivity).

Affected: LibreOffice >= 26.2, < 26.2.7 and >= 26.8, < 26.8.2. Fixed: 26.2.7 and 26.8.2.

Advisory and fix

DateEvent
2026-11-16Advisory published by The Document Foundation
2026-11-16Fixed in LibreOffice 26.2.7 and 26.8.2

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post by cloning the repository and running three commands:

Full PoC, detection rules, and evidence: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-104692

entry.content:
The advisory

Node.js shipped security releases on November 2026 covering several HTTP/2 vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-123874 stood out: a use-after-free in the HTTP/2 server that lets an unauthenticated client corrupt heap memory when the application serves files with stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD(). CVSS 7.5 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H). The fix commit included an in-tree test, but it used duplexPair (an in-process mock transport) and --expose-gc, so it never sent traffic over the network.

I built a network-based PoC that sends real HTTP/2 frames, confirmed the heap-use-after-free with AddressSanitizer, and captured the attack traffic in a pcap.

PoC, detection rules, and live pcap: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-123874

How Node.js serves files over HTTP/2

To understand the bug, you need to know how respondWithFile() works under the hood, and why it behaves differently from the more common respond() or pipe() patterns.

Node.js HTTP/2 is built on nghttp2, the C library that handles frame parsing, flow control, and stream state. On top of that, Node.js adds its own C++ layer (Http2Session, Http2Stream) that bridges nghttp2 into V8’s event loop and garbage collector. This layer is where the bug lives.

When a Node.js HTTP/2 server calls stream.respondWithFile(path), the file is not piped through JavaScript. Instead, the native layer opens the file through a FileHandle, reads chunks into ArrayBuffer backing stores via FileHandle::ReadStart(), and pushes them onto the session’s outgoing_buffers_ queue as NgHttp2StreamWrite structs. Each struct holds two references: a req_wrap (the write request) and a buffer_owner (ownership of the backing store memory). The session then calls uv_write to send the buffered data to the TCP socket.

This is efficient. The file data flows from disk to the network through native buffers, bypassing JavaScript entirely. But there is a gap: NgHttp2StreamWrite does not hold a reference to the Http2Stream itself. The struct knows about the write request and the buffer, but not about the stream that originated the response.

In normal operation this is fine. The HTTP/2 session holds the stream, and the stream lives as long as the session or until the response finishes. The JavaScript application typically holds a reference to the stream too, since it called respondWithFile() on it. But with respondWithFile(), the response continues asynchronously at the native level, and the JavaScript reference can go out of scope before the writes complete.

HTTP/2 gives clients a tool to break the assumption that the stream outlives its writes: RST_STREAM. Any client can cancel any stream at any time by sending a RST_STREAM frame with error code 0x8 (CANCEL). The server must honor it.

The vulnerable code

Here is the path through src/node_http2.cc before the fix. When OnSendData pushes a buffer for a respondWithFile() response:

The NgHttp2StreamWrite struct (from src/node_http2.h) had no Http2Stream field:

Compare with the fix:

One field. That is the entire difference between a safe server and a use-after-free.

The race

With respondWithFile(), the server pushes large file buffers onto the outgoing queue and starts writing them to the socket asynchronously via uv_write. The write is non-blocking; libuv assembles an array of iovec entries (each pointing to a backing store and giving its length) and passes them to the kernel’s writev syscall when the socket file descriptor becomes writable. For a large file, the write queue may contain dozens of iovec entries spanning megabytes of data, and the kernel may take several event loop iterations to drain them all.

Now consider what happens when a client sends RST_STREAM (CANCEL) while those writes are pending:

  1. The server processes RST_STREAM and closes the stream.
  2. The stream’s JavaScript wrapper loses its references.
  3. V8’s garbage collector runs and collects the Http2Stream C++ object.
  4. Http2Stream::CompleteDestroyCleanup runs, destroying the SimpleWriteWrap objects and freeing the backing stores (BackingStore::~BackingStore calls free).
  5. The pending uv_write callback fires. writev reads from the iovec, which still points to the freed backing store.

Step 5 is a textbook use-after-free. The iovec contains a pointer and a length for a 64 KB buffer that no longer exists.

Building the lab

The challenge was making the race reliable. Understanding the bug is one thing; observing it is another. On localhost, TCP writes complete almost instantly because there is no network latency; the kernel socket buffer is large enough to absorb the entire write in one writev call before the event loop returns to process the stream destruction. Without intervention, even if GC frees the backing store, the freed region still contains the original file data (the allocator does not zero it), and writev reads it successfully. The corruption is invisible.

I needed three things: a way to force GC to run between the RST_STREAM and the write callback, a file large enough to keep the write queue busy across multiple event loop iterations, and AddressSanitizer to poison freed memory so the access becomes observable as a crash instead of a silent read.

The lab server (lab/server.js) is a minimal HTTP/2 server that serves a 64 MB file via respondWithFile(). It runs with --expose-gc and --max-old-space-size=64 (constraining V8’s heap to 64 MB), and a timer calls global.gc() every 5 milliseconds. These are not default settings, and they would not be present in production. They exist to close the race window: forcing frequent garbage collection makes the stream wrapper get collected while writes are still pending, and the large file keeps writes queued long enough for GC to run.

The ASAN build was compiled from the Node.js 24.22.2 source with ./configure --enable-asan and clang 18 on Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64). AddressSanitizer replaces the standard allocator with one that quarantines freed memory and fills it with the poison byte 0xfd. When writev reads from a freed backing store, it hits poisoned memory and ASAN traps the access, printing a detailed report with the allocation, free, and access stack traces. Without ASAN, the same read would succeed silently because the freed memory still holds the file data, and the program would continue with corrupted internal state.

The crash

On the first run, the ASAN server crashed. From evidence/target-asan-crash.txt:

The access: writev reads 12,752 bytes from an iovec pointing into a freed 64 KB region.

The free: CompleteDestroyCleanup is the callback that runs when the Http2Stream is garbage-collected. It destroys the write wraps, which free their backing stores.

The allocation: FileHandle::ReadStart() allocated the buffer when reading the file for respondWithFile().

This is the complete causal chain. The buffer was created for the file response, freed when the stream was garbage-collected after RST_STREAM, and read by the pending socket write. The ASAN shadow memory around the buggy address is all fd (freed heap region):

The PoC result from evidence/poc-vuln-asan.txt:

Negative control

The same PoC against Node.js 24.22.3 (the first patched version):

Five rounds, 2,500 streams opened and reset, zero crashes. The fix works.

Impact

The advisory rates this CVSS 7.5 High with an availability impact of High and no confidentiality or integrity impact. That matches what I observed: the use-after-free corrupts heap memory and crashes the server (denial of service). The read-after-free does not leak data to the attacker because the corrupted data stays inside the server process, in the writev iovec, and is never sent back to the client. The corruption happens inside libuv’s write path, in kernel-side writev, reading from an iovec that points to freed userspace memory.

Any Node.js HTTP/2 server that calls respondWithFile() or respondWithFD() is affected. These APIs are the recommended way to serve static files over HTTP/2 in Node.js. The http2 module documentation explicitly suggests respondWithFile() for serving static content because it avoids the overhead of reading the file through JavaScript streams. Web frameworks and static file servers built on Node.js HTTP/2 are the most likely targets.

The attack requires no authentication. The client sends only standard HTTP/2 frames: HEADERS to open streams and RST_STREAM to cancel them. No special headers, no crafted payloads, no session state. Any HTTP/2 client library can produce these frames, and there is nothing unusual about RST_STREAM CANCEL in normal HTTP/2 traffic (browsers send it when navigating away from a page).

In practice, the bug is harder to trigger without the lab’s forced GC and constrained heap. A production server with a large default heap (around 1.5 GB) and no --expose-gc will have less frequent garbage collection, making the race window narrower. The race requires GC to run between the RST_STREAM processing (which drops the stream references) and the libuv write callback (which reads from the buffer). On localhost, TCP writes complete almost instantly, so GC rarely gets a chance. Over a real network with latency, the write takes longer and the window widens. Under sustained load with many concurrent connections and large file transfers, natural memory pressure can trigger GC at the right moment. Without ASAN, the corruption is silent unless the freed region is reallocated and overwritten before writev reads it, or unless the heap metadata around the freed region is corrupted enough to crash the allocator.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Heap-use-after-free (ASAN, crash, 1/1)Provenevidence/target-asan-crash.txt
Root cause confirmed by ASAN stack traceProvenevidence/target-asan-crash.txt
Attack is unauthenticated (AV:N, PR:N)ProvenNo credentials in PoC
Patched version unaffected (0/5)Confirmedevidence/poc-patched.txt
Remote code executionNot reachedCVSS vector is C:N/I:N/A:H

Detection

Two experimental / minimally validated rule sets, each tested against the canonical attack capture and one benign fixture only:

Suricata (detection/cve-2026-123874.rules): alerts on a burst of 20 or more HTTP/2 RST_STREAM CANCEL frames from a single client within 10 seconds. Not specific to this CVE. Requires Suricata 7.0+ with HTTP/2 app-layer enabled; TLS inspection needed for h2 (as opposed to h2c).

Sigma (detection/cve-2026-123874-crash.yml): detects a Node.js HTTP/2 server crash (ASAN heap-use-after-free, SIGSEGV, or SIGABRT) with concurrent ERR_HTTP2_STREAM_CANCEL in the application log. Requires ASAN builds or crash-producing heap layouts to fire.

The fix

Commit 8e100ac by Matteo Collina adds one field to NgHttp2StreamWrite:

This BaseObjectPtr is a release-prevented reference. As long as any NgHttp2StreamWrite in outgoing_buffers_ holds a pointer to the stream, V8’s garbage collector cannot collect it. The stream stays alive until its write buffers are consumed and dequeued, at which point the BaseObjectPtr destructor releases the reference and the stream can be collected normally.

The fix also simplifies HasWritesOnSocketForStream to use wr.stream.get() instead of walking the session’s stream map, since the stream reference is now directly available in each write buffer.

Advisory and fix

DateEvent
November 2026Node.js security release advisory published
November 2026Node.js 24.22.3 and 26.13.1 released with the fix
2026-11-16Reproduction and write-up

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post by running the PoC from the repository. The ASAN proof requires building Node.js from source with --enable-asan on a Linux x86_64 host.

The full evidence, detection rules, and live pcap are in the repository: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-123874.

What’s this?

Pillow 13.0.0 shipped on October 19, 2026 with a batch of security fixes. GHSA-xcvg-w56q-r89m caught my eye: a heap buffer overflow in the libtiff TIFF encoder, triggered when user-supplied EXIF metadata overrides geometry tags during image re-save. CVSS 4.0: 8.4 (High). The advisory mentioned out-of-bounds read and write, but no public PoC existed.

I built one. The result: upload a 204-byte JPEG, get 8,192 bytes of server heap in the TIFF that comes back. One HTTP POST, no credentials, 100% reliable.

PoC, detection rules, and live pcap: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-128067

The root cause

When Pillow saves an image as TIFF using the libtiff encoder, TiffImagePlugin._save sets geometry tags (ImageWidth, ImageLength, PlanarConfiguration) from the actual image dimensions. Then a merge loop overwrites them with whatever the caller passed via tiffinfo=, exif=, or the source image’s own IFD. SamplesPerPixel is never explicitly set for single-band modes.

The row buffer is allocated from the real image: for a 64x64 grayscale image, that’s calloc(64, 1) = 64 bytes. But TIFFWriteScanline reads a scanline sized by the tag-described geometry. With SamplesPerPixel=3 injected through EXIF, libtiff reads 192-byte scanlines from a 64-byte buffer.

The extra 128 bytes per row come from whatever sits behind the buffer on the heap. And because the output TIFF is returned to the caller, those bytes go straight back to the attacker.

Three impacts

The PoC demonstrates three variants from a single attack surface:

Heap data leak. EXIF SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB makes the encoder read 192-byte rows from a 64-byte buffer. 128 bytes of heap per row × 64 rows = 8,192 bytes of server memory per request, returned in a valid TIFF image.

Heap write. Adding Predictor=2 to the EXIF makes libtiff apply horizontal differencing to each row before compression. On libtiff < 4.7.1, horDiff8 differences the row in place — rewriting the 128 heap bytes past the buffer on every row. On libtiff 4.7.1+ (official Pillow wheels), it works on a private copy, so Predictor=2 is only an additional over-read.

Crash. EXIF ImageWidth=134217728 (128 MiB) makes libtiff attempt a 128 MiB scanline read from a 64-byte buffer. Instant SIGSEGV.

The information disclosure angle

The leak variant is the most interesting. The attacker sends one HTTP POST with a 204-byte JPEG and gets a TIFF containing 8 KB of the target’s heap. The leaked data contains heap metadata, pointer-like values from mmap’d regions, and whatever data structures the allocator placed adjacent to the encoder’s buffer.

This is not a crash — the server returns HTTP 200 with a valid TIFF. It works on every request. It requires no credentials. And the leaked data changes between requests as the heap layout shifts.

ASAN confirms

I built Pillow and libtiff 4.7.0 with AddressSanitizer to get the exact trace:

The buffer is allocated at encode.c:293 (64 bytes for the 64-pixel row). The overflow starts at the very first byte past it — tif_lzw.c:1163 in LZWEncode.

The vulnerable pattern

The app doesn’t have to do anything exotic. This is the vulnerable code:

The key line is exif=img.getexif() — it passes the attacker’s EXIF metadata through to the TIFF encoder, where the geometry tags override the buffer dimensions.

The fix

Pillow 13.0.0 added a check in ImagingLibTiffEncode that compares TIFFScanlineSize64() against state->bytes before writing any scanlines. If the tag-described scanline is larger than the buffer, it returns “encoder error -8” instead of proceeding.

Fix commit: ec5f1cb

Reliability

10-round test against the distro build (Pillow 12.3.0, libtiff 4.7.0):

  • leak: 10/10
  • write: 10/10
  • crash: 10/10

All three variants fire on every single request.

What to do

Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0:

If you’re on any version from 2.3.0 through 12.3.0 and your application passes user-supplied metadata to the TIFF encoder, you’re vulnerable.

Reproduce it

References

  • GHSA-xcvg-w56q-r89m (GitHub Security Advisory)
  • CVE-2026-128067
  • Fix commit ec5f1cb
  • Pillow 13.0.0 release notes
entry.summary: Upload a 204-byte JPEG to any Python service re-saving images as TIFF with Pillow < 13.0.0 and get 8 KB of server heap back. The heap overflow in ImagingLibTiffEncode happens because EXIF geometry tags override the encoder's buffer dimensions.

entry.content:
The advisory for CVE-2026-116779 says that a SIP MESSAGE can make FreeSWITCH execute commands with the privileges of its own process: arbitrary OS commands, disclosure of configuration and credentials, full call control. It is rated CVSS 9.8, it has been exploited in the wild, and it was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09.

I reproduced the first part of that on 2026-11-14, on FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 built from the upstream tag. One MESSAGE whose To header starts with api+system ran id; hostname on the target as the service user, and the target sent me the output in a SIP MESSAGE of its own. I used no secret: a vanilla install ships a directory user called default with no password, and that account is enough to pass MESSAGE authentication. FreeSWITCH 1.11.3 answers the same MESSAGE with 403 Forbidden. I did not read configuration files, I did not touch a call, and I did not run the exploit over UDP.

This is a reproduction of a disclosed bug, not a discovery. What I add is the material to check it yourself: a PoC that is one Python file and speaks SIP without a library, a lab that builds both versions from source, a live capture and experimental Suricata and Sigma rules. The runs also turned up four things a defender should know. The account that needs no password. Three different API commands through the same hole. An external profile that executes the command without telling the sender. And a stock log that says nothing at all about a successful exploit.

Repo with the PoC, the lab, the capture and the rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-116779.

The target: MESSAGE, profiles and chat interfaces

FreeSWITCH is an open-source telephony platform, and SIP is how most of the outside world talks to it. The SIP side lives in mod_sofia, which runs one or more profiles. The vanilla configuration has two, internal on port 5060 and external on port 5080.

SIP is not only calls. MESSAGE is the method for instant messages: a request with a From, a To and a body. FreeSWITCH accepts it on any profile that has chat enabled, and chat is enabled by default on both stock profiles. Since 1.10.7 the sender also has to pass Digest authentication first, by default.

Inside the server, a message is handed to a chat interface. Modules register these under a name, and the name decides who gets the message. sip delivers to a registered SIP user. mod_dptools registers one called api, and that one does not deliver anything: it takes the destination address, runs it as a FreeSWITCH API command, and sends the command’s output back to the sender as a message. The API includes global_getvar, which reads a global variable, lua, which runs Lua, and system, which runs a shell command.

So the server has, by design, a messaging endpoint that executes commands. The question for this CVE is who can address a message to it.

The advisory gives no figure for exposed servers and I have none, so I give none. The CVSS 3.1 vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, and the SSVC assessment recorded for the CVE is exploitation active, automatable, total impact.

The split at the plus sign

The answer is in sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message(), the function in mod_sofia that receives every inbound MESSAGE. I found it by reading the fix commit and following the call chain in the v1.11.2 tree. These are the lines that matter, each quoted on its own with its place in that tree. They are not one contiguous listing; the links go to the full code.

to_user is the user part of the To header. If it contains a + that is not its first character, the handler cuts it there. The left half is copied into proto. The right half becomes the destination address. About 140 lines later the handler calls switch_core_chat_send(proto, event), and the core looks up a chat interface with that name and calls it.

What the code should do is decide for itself which chat interface an inbound SIP message goes to. What it does is let the To header decide. Nothing between line 4874 and line 5018 limits which name a SIP peer may put on the left of the +.

Now name api. api_chat_send() URL-decodes the address, splits it at the first space, and calls switch_api_execute() with the two halves as command and argument. Then it sends whatever the command wrote back through the sip chat interface, to the address the MESSAGE came from. With system as the command, mod_commands passes the argument to a shell.

Put together: a MESSAGE with To: <sip:api+system%20id@domain> runs id on the server, and the server posts the result back.

What an attacker needs

Four conditions, three for execution and one for comfort.

  1. A SIP MESSAGE reaches a profile with chat enabled. That is the default.
  2. The sender passes MESSAGE authentication. That is on by default too.
  3. The user part of the To header starts with api+. The Request-URI does not matter here, because to_user comes from the To header. The compare ignores case and happens after sofia-sip has unescaped the user part, a detail that comes back in the detection section.
  4. To receive the output, the sender has to be registered on the internal profile under the From address it uses. Without a registration the command still runs. Only the reply is dropped.

The second condition looks like it should end the “no privileges required” story. On a vanilla install it does not. conf/vanilla/directory/default/default.xml ships a user named default that has no parameters and no password, and sofia_reg_parse_auth() returns AUTH_OK for it. The Digest handshake still takes place on the wire. The client still computes a response. The password that goes into the hash is the empty string.

I call that “no secret” and not “no authentication”, because the two are different claims. An install without the default user, or with allow-empty-password=false, does not have this door, and I did not test one. What I did test is that an ordinary account works just as well: any user that may send a MESSAGE can address one to api.

A target that does not come as an image

The first obstacle was mundane. I found no official FreeSWITCH Docker image to pull, so setup.py builds both versions from the upstream tags in a Debian bookworm container: v1.11.2 at commit 3f13ad1b1d32 and v1.11.3 at ef32e205295e. The build stops unless git rev-parse HEAD and git describe --tags --exact-match agree with those pins. sofia-sip and spandsp come from the FreeSWITCH forks, pinned by commit as well. On a 16-core machine the first image took 150 seconds and the second 90.

A source build of a telephony server wants a lot of libraries, and I did not give it all of them. mod_av, mod_signalwire and mod_verto are left out because they need ffmpeg, libks and signalwire-c. None is on the path of this bug. It does mean that the sibling fix for mod_verto cannot be tested in this lab, and I make no claim about it. The stock vars.xml asks a public STUN server for the external address at start-up, and a lab with a known-vulnerable service should not be calling third parties, so both values point at the local address. FreeSWITCH runs as the user freeswitch, as the distribution packages run it. A source install started as root would run the attacker’s commands as root.

One deviation shapes everything that follows. The lab publishes SIP on 127.0.0.1 of the Docker host only, and my laptop reaches it through an ssh port-forward. ssh forwards TCP. So every exploit run in this post is SIP over TCP. Stock FreeSWITCH listens on UDP as well, on the same ports, and I did not run the exploit over UDP.

setup.py prints what it started, so the run itself shows the versions (evidence/setup.txt):

The two enable-chat-api-proto lines are a cheap sanity check. The fix introduces a profile parameter with that name. The string is absent from mod_sofia.so in the 1.11.2 build and present in 1.11.3, where the shipped profile mentions it only in a comment.

Walking one run

poc.py does everything on one TCP connection, and capture/exploit.pcap in the repository is that connection, recorded live on the target’s network interface. It has 28 packets and spans 63 milliseconds.

OPTIONS, no credentials. The server answers 200 OK with a User-Agent of FreeSWITCH-mod_sofia/1.11.2-release[...] and a Contact of sip:172.31.79.12. That gives the version and the SIP domain. It is also everything check.py does: one OPTIONS, a verdict from the banner, and no MESSAGE. The check says “confidence: medium” and never more, because a banner can be changed and it cannot see the profile’s settings.

REGISTER as default. The server answers 401 with a Digest challenge, the PoC answers the challenge with an empty password, and the server says 200 OK. Why register at all, if the bug is in MESSAGE? Because of where the output goes. api_chat_send() replies through the sip chat interface, and that interface finds its destination by looking the address up in the internal profile’s registrations. No registration, no reply. I want the reply, because the reply is the proof.

MESSAGE, twice. The first one carries no credentials and gets 407 Proxy Authentication Required. The second is the same request with a Proxy-Authorization header for default, and the server answers 202 Accepted. In the capture these are packets 14, 15, 17 and 19. Packet 17 is the trigger.

Inside the server. The handler splits the To user, finds api, and hands over the rest. I cannot show this step directly on the vulnerable build, because it logs nothing on this path. I see it by what happens next, and by what the patched build does at the same place.

MESSAGE, from the server. Packet 20 is a new request, from the target to my registered contact. Its From address is the api+system... address I wrote into the To header. Its body is the output of my command.

The proof

The command the PoC sends is benign: id; hostname; echo <marker> | tee <file in /tmp>. The marker contains an arithmetic expression, $((9260*3427)) in this run. The PoC sends the expression as text. Only a shell can turn it into a number, so a reply that contains the product was produced by a shell on the target. This is run 5cdca241 (evidence/poc-vulnerable.txt):

Read it from the top. The To user decodes to an API command line, system followed by a shell command. The PoC percent-encodes every character that is not a letter or a digit, which is why the request line is so hard on the eyes. The server accepts the MESSAGE and, a few milliseconds later, sends one back. Its From header is the server’s own rendering of the address I sent, already unescaped. X-FS-Sending-Message is a FreeSWITCH-specific header, and it turns out to be a useful one for detection. Then the body: the id of the service user, the container’s hostname, and 31734020, which is 9260 times 3427.

The body is evidence from the target, but it arrived through my own script. So I also looked from the other side. This is the file the command wrote, read from inside the container after the run (evidence/target-marker-vulnerable.txt):

The file’s timestamp is 12:39:34.453 by the lab host’s clock. In the capture, the trigger is at 12:39:34.450 and the reply at 12:39:34.454. The file was written in the four milliseconds between them.

Five rounds out of five returned output (evidence/poc-vulnerable-rounds5.txt). There is no race to win here. It is a logic flaw and it fires every time.

The negative control

The same script, the same MESSAGE, against FreeSWITCH 1.11.3 (evidence/poc-patched.txt):

No marker file exists on the patched target (evidence/target-marker-patched.txt), and the server wrote down what it refused (evidence/freeswitch-patched.log, line 1227):

That log line also closes the one step I could not see on 1.11.2. It comes from sofia_presence.c:4884, a few lines below the split, and it quotes my command as the thing addressed to the api chat proto. The fixed build stops exactly where the vulnerable build went on.

Not only system

system is the loudest API command, not the only one. The PoC takes any API command line with --api. A configuration variable (evidence/poc-vulnerable-api-getvar.txt):

1234 is the stock value of default_password. That is one global variable, read back over SIP. I did not go further into configuration files or the user directory, so the advisory’s “disclosure of configuration and credentials” is shown here only to that extent.

Inline Lua, where mod_lua is loaded, which it is in the stock configuration (evidence/poc-vulnerable-api-lua.txt):

The script asks for _VERSION and for io.popen('id'). Both come back. This matters for anyone who thinks of mitigating by removing system: the Lua standard library is a second way to the shell.

And the passwordless account is a convenience, not a requirement. With --user 1000 --password 1234, a stock directory user with the stock password, the result is the same as with default (evidence/poc-vulnerable-user1000.txt).

The run that looked like a miss

Then I pointed the PoC at port 15080, the external profile of the vulnerable target. This is what came back (evidence/poc-vulnerable-external.txt):

202 Accepted, then silence, and my own script reports that it observed no impact. Taken alone, that output says the external profile is not exploitable. The target tells a different story. The marker file of that run is there (evidence/target-marker-vulnerable-after-external.txt):

And this time the server log has something to say (evidence/freeswitch-vulnerable-after-external.log):

The command ran. FreeSWITCH then tried to send the output, looked for the destination among the registrations of the internal profile, found nobody to send to, and logged the whole reply as an error: the command, the id output, the marker, and “Nobody to send to”.

So the external profile gives blind execution. An attacker gets no output on that connection, and does not need any. I did not try the combination of registering on internal and triggering on external, so I cannot say whether the output can be recovered that way.

The quiet log

That error is the only thing the vulnerable server ever logged about any of this, and it logged it because the exploit half failed.

After the main run, the one where the reply was delivered, the target’s freeswitch.log has no line about the MESSAGE, none about the API command, none about the shell (evidence/freeswitch-vulnerable.log). The only line it gained during the run is mod_voicemail.c:4068 Event Thread Started, which says nothing about a MESSAGE or a command. This holds for the stock log settings of my lab build, and I did not try others.

For incident response that is uncomfortable. On a vulnerable server, the clean exploit is the invisible one. If you find Chat proto [api] errors in a 1.11.2 log, you are looking at the attempts that could not deliver their output, and each of those lines contains the command and what it printed.

What this shows, and what it does not

ClaimStatus
OS command execution on 1.11.2 through a MESSAGE to api+system, output returned over SIP, no secret usedProven
1.11.3 rejects the same MESSAGE with 403 Forbidden, logs it, and nothing runsConfirmed
Other API commands run too: global_getvar default_password returned the target’s valueProven
Inline Lua through mod_lua with the standard library (io.popen)Proven
An ordinary account (stock user 1000) works like defaultProven
The external profile of 1.11.2 accepts the MESSAGE and runs the command blindProven on the target side only
The external profile of 1.11.3 answers 403 ForbiddenConfirmed
A successful exploit with a delivered reply leaves no line in the stock freeswitch.logProven for this lab’s stock log settings
Reading configuration files and credentials beyond one global variable; call controlNot reached: not attempted
The exploit over UDPNot reached: not attempted, the lab publishes TCP only
Output returned when the trigger goes to the external profileNot reached: one run, reply dropped; registering on internal first was not tried
The exploit with no account at allNot reached: not attempted
The mod_verto route, which has its own fixNot reached: mod_verto is not built in this lab

Proven means the evidence file is in the repository. Confirmed means the negative control was run. Not reached means not shown here. It does not mean not possible. The README has the same table with a file for every row.

The advisory says command execution with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process. For OS commands, that is what I saw. The rest of its list I did not test.

Detection

The repository ships three Suricata rules and one Sigma rule. All four are experimental / minimally validated. Each passed its validator, fired on the canonical artifact and stayed quiet on one benign fixture, and that is the whole of the testing. I ran no payload variations and measured no false-positive rate.

The Suricata rules look at SIP over TCP. Two match an inbound MESSAGE with api+ or api%2B in the To header. The third matches the reply: an outbound MESSAGE with X-FS-Sending-Message and api+ in its From header, which means a command ran and its output left the building. On the exploit capture they give three alerts, and none on a capture of an ordinary OPTIONS, REGISTER and MESSAGE exchange.

The Sigma rule reads freeswitch.log and matches two lines you have already seen in this post: the rejection warning of the fixed build and the Chat proto [api] error of the vulnerable build.

Know the limits before you rely on any of it.

  • The selector can be spelled in ways the rules do not cover. The server unescapes the To user before it compares, and it ignores case. The rules cover the literal api+ and api%2B. They do not cover percent-encoded letters such as %61pi+.
  • TCP only. The rules are written and tested for TCP. FreeSWITCH also listens on UDP, and the UDP variants were not tested.
  • The log rule is blind to the clean exploit. A delivered reply leaves no log line on a vulnerable build, so the Sigma rule sees only failed deliveries and patched servers. On a vulnerable server you need the network view.
  • Plaintext only. SIP over TLS needs decryption in front of the sensor.

The rules, their documentation and the test commands are in detection/.

The fix

The fix is one condition in the right place. In v1.11.3, directly after the split:

If the sender named api and the profile does not carry the new flag, the handler logs the warning shown above, answers 403 Forbidden and returns. The flag is set by a new profile parameter, enable-chat-api-proto. It is off unless set, and the vanilla profiles ship it commented out.

It works because it moves the decision back to the operator. Whether a SIP peer may reach the API through a message is now a property of the profile, and the To header no longer decides it. The gate is specific to the name api. I did not look at what other chat interfaces a peer can name, and the parameter cuts both ways: on a fixed build with enable-chat-api-proto=true, a profile runs API commands from MESSAGE by design.

For operators the fix is the update to 1.11.3. Removing the passwordless default user is worth doing, but it closes only the no-secret path, because any account that may send a MESSAGE is enough on a vulnerable build.

Advisory and fix

DateEvent
2026-08-28Commit date of the v1.11.3 tag, the first fixed release, as the build prints it in its version string
2026-11-09Added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
2026-11-14My reproduction runs (UTC)

The fix is commit 7015f6a73ab3, PR #3135. The table holds only the dates I can source. The advisory is GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p. It lists FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 and earlier as affected and credits Örn Arnarson as reporter and Gunnlaugur as analyst.

Reproduce it

You need Python 3 and Docker on a Linux x86_64 host with about 3 GB of free disk. If Docker is on another machine, add --lab-host user@host to the setup.py commands and the lab runs there, reached through an ssh port-forward. That is the mode every run in this post used.

check.py answers VERDICT: VULNERABLE for the first target without sending a MESSAGE. The first poc.py run ends in RESULT: VULNERABLE. OS command execution through SIP MESSAGE observed. Exit 0. The second, against 1.11.3, ends in RESULT: impact NOT observed. Exit 1. The README lists every step with its expected output, and evidence/INDEX.md lists every evidence file with the command that produced it and the claim it supports. Run it only against the lab.

References

  • Repository: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-116779
  • Advisory: GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p
  • Fix commit: 7015f6a73ab3, PR #3135
  • Vulnerable function: sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() at tag v1.11.2
  • The api chat interface: api_chat_send() at tag v1.11.2
entry.summary: CVE-2026-116779: FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 runs OS commands from one SIP MESSAGE addressed to api+system. CVSS 9.8, exploited in the wild. Lab, PoC, pcap, rules.

entry.content:
The CVE record for CVE-2026-125350 says the bug “allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page”. Google’s advisory of 2026-11-09 adds that an exploit exists in the wild, and the CVE was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10.

I reproduced less than that, and this post says how much. An XML document with an XSLT stylesheet, served over HTTP, crashes the sandboxed renderer of stock Google Chrome 157.0.8103.38 on Linux, with no flag. The same page does nothing to 157.0.8103.50. On a sanitizer build one revision before the fix, the crash is a heap use after free in libxslt. I did not attempt code execution.

The trigger is not new. Its two shapes follow the two cases of the crash test that the fix commit added to Chromium. What I add is a lab of stock Chrome builds pinned by checksum, the raw output of every run, the sanitizer’s allocation stacks for both cases with the reason in libxslt’s code why each leaves a stale object behind, a check that does not trigger the bug, live captures, and tested Suricata and YARA rules. All of it is in the repository: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-125350.

The target: XSLT inside the renderer

Chrome runs XSLT with a bundled copy of libxslt, and it runs it inside the renderer process. The page in this post needs no script to reach that code: the browser loads an XML document, finds an xml-stylesheet processing instruction in it, fetches the stylesheet and applies it. The user does one thing, which is to open the URL.

The advisory names Google Chrome only and gives no figures on scale, so I give none. The CVSS 3.1 vector from CISA is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, 8.8 High.

A cache and a pointer that outlives it

The bug is in one function, xsltTestCompMatchDirect() in pattern.c. libxslt uses it as a shortcut for patterns with two predicates in a row, such as book[p][q]. It evaluates //book[p][q] once per document and caches the resulting node-set object in a slot of the transform context that belongs to the pattern, together with the document it was computed for.

On entry the function copies the cached pointer into a local variable. If the node it is asked about sits in another document, it evaluates the pattern again with xmlXPathEval(), frees the old object through that local variable and stores the new one.

The trouble is what the evaluation can do in between. A predicate that reads a global variable not yet computed makes libxslt evaluate the variable’s body on the spot. If that body runs an xsl:number whose count pattern uses the same slot, the function is entered a second time. The nested call frees the cached object and installs another.

Back in the outer call, the local variable still points at the freed object. xmlXPathFreeObject() reads its type field, which is the use after free, may free what its nodesetval field points to, and frees the object a second time. The fix commit’s message describes the same thing:

xsltTestCompMatchDirect read the cached node-set from the transform context’s runtime extras before calling xmlXPathEval, then freed that pointer afterwards. The evaluation can re-enter the function for the same cache slot (e.g. via a lazily evaluated global variable whose value runs xsl:number), and the nested call may free and replace the cached object, resulting in a double free.

What the stylesheet has to do

Five conditions have to hold.

  1. XSLT is enabled in the browser.
  2. An xsl:number count pattern has two consecutive predicates, one of which reads a global variable.
  3. A stale object is already in the pattern’s slot when the outer call starts.
  4. Three nodes sit in three documents, so that neither call sees the cached document: the source document and two loaded with document().
  5. The variable has not been computed before the predicate reads it.

The third condition is the one that needs a trick, because xsl:number clears its count pattern’s cache after every use. Two paths leave an object behind anyway, and they are the same two that the fix commit’s crash test uses.

  • union: xsltCompMatchClearCache() clears only the first alternative of a | b, so a second alternative that is matched directly keeps its object.
  • import: slot numbers of template patterns in an imported stylesheet are shifted on import, those of xsl:number patterns are not. A count pattern in a second import then shares a slot with a template pattern of the first, whose cache is never cleared.

This is the stylesheet my PoC serves for the union shape, as the PoC prints it (evidence/poc_stable-vuln_union.txt):

Read it with the conditions in mind. $outer numbers the book of the source document, and the direct match caches a node-set for the second alternative of nothing | book[...][...]. Then $outer numbers the book of second.xml. That is a new document, so the outer call takes its copy of the cached pointer and starts evaluating the pattern again. The second predicate reads $inner, which has not been computed yet. Its body loads third.xml and runs the same xsl:number, so the nested call frees the cached object. The outer call comes back holding a pointer to freed memory and frees it again.

A count pattern with a single predicate never enters the function. The PoC has a control variant for that, and it renders normally on the vulnerable build (evidence/poc_stable-vuln_control.txt).

The browser that would not run it

One lab target did not behave like the others. This is the union page against Chrome for Testing 157.0.8103.38 as shipped (evidence/poc_cft-noflag_union.txt):

The browser shows the XML and never asks for the stylesheet. That build ships with XSLT off, so a page cannot reach the bug there. With --enable-features=XSLT it crashes like the others, but a lab that needs a switch says nothing about a default install.

The stable-channel .deb is different: 157.0.8103.38 runs XSLT with no switch. So the lab’s main pair is the stable package at 157.0.8103.38 and at 157.0.8103.50, unpacked and run headless in Docker with Chrome’s own sandbox on. One limit belongs here. The lab browsers run with their compiled-in feature defaults and never fetch Google’s live field-trial configuration, which can switch features on or off on a user’s machine. I did not test that.

The crash

poc.py plays the attacker’s web server and the user’s click. It uses the DevTools port only to open the URL and to read what the browser says about its renderer. The payload travels over HTTP like any page. Against stock Chrome 157.0.8103.38 (evidence/poc_stable-vuln_union.txt):

The [http] lines are the target’s own requests: the document, the stylesheet, then the two documents that document() pulls in. After third.xml the browser reports that its renderer is gone. Twenty rounds per variant gave 20/20 crashes on 157.0.8103.38.

The verdict above comes from the browser. The renderer also left its own record, a Crashpad minidump (evidence/crash_stable-vuln.txt):

A ptype=renderer process of version 157.0.8103.38 died with SIGTRAP. The import variant dies with SIGSEGV. And that is all a stock build tells you, because it ships no symbols: the frames are module offsets.

Getting function names

To see which function is at fault I needed a build that names its frames. Chromium publishes AddressSanitizer snapshots of its main branch, and two of them sit exactly where I wanted them: r1738200, the parent of the fix commit, and r1738201, the fix commit itself. The same served documents, against r1738200 (evidence/crash_asan-vuln.txt, report 1 of 2):

Read the “freed by” stack from the bottom. The outer call is inside xmlXPathEval() at pattern.c:565. The variable lookup runs the global variable’s body. A nested xsltTestCompMatchDirect() frees the object at line 585. The read at the top is the outer call, back from the evaluation with its stale pointer, in the same line 585.

The second report, for the import shape, has the same read and the same free. What differs is where the stale object was allocated (evidence/crash_asan-vuln.txt, report 2 of 2):

In the union case the object was allocated while numbering a node. Here it was allocated by template matching, in xsltGetTemplate(), and later freed through an xsl:number pattern. That is the shared slot.

I want to be exact about what this report is. It comes from a Chromium main-branch snapshot, not from Chrome 157. Lines 565 and 585 are the same there as at tag 157.0.8103.38, but the stock 157 binaries give me no function names. On stock 157, the crash is tied to this function by the negative control and by the sanitizer pair, whose two revisions differ by exactly the fix commit.

The negative control

The same poc.py, the same documents, against Chrome 157.0.8103.50 (evidence/poc_stable-patched_union.txt):

The patched browser makes the same four requests, finishes the transform and returns its text. It wrote no crash report, and the sanitizer build at the fix commit printed no report (evidence/crash_stable-patched.txt, evidence/crash_asan-patched.txt):

Twenty rounds per variant against 157.0.8103.50 gave 0/20.

What this shows, and what it does not

ClaimStatus
Opening the served XML document crashes the renderer of stock Google Chrome 157.0.8103.38 (stable .deb, Linux x86_64, sandbox on, no feature switch)Confirmed
The same PoC does nothing to 157.0.8103.50Confirmed
The bug is a heap use after free in xmlXPathFreeObject() on a stale pointer held by xsltTestCompMatchDirect(), freed by a nested call reached through a lazily evaluated global variableConfirmed on ASAN r1738200 against r1738201, not on Chrome 157
The trigger fires every timeProven
XSLT runs by default in stable 157.0.8103.38 with compiled-in defaults and is off in Chrome for Testing 157.0.8103.38 as shippedProven
Code execution in the renderer (the disclosed impact), or any controlled use of the freed objectNot reached: not attempted
Windows and macOS builds, and versions other than 157.0.8103.38 and 157.0.8103.50Not reached: not tested
The documents served from a non-loopback originNot reached: every run fetched them from http://127.0.0.1:38080
Which variant matches which of the two bug reports the fix closes, and which one the exploit in the wild usedNot reached: unknown and not claimed

Proven means the evidence file is in the repository. Confirmed means the negative control was run. Not reached means not shown here; it does not mean not possible. The README has the full table with a file for every row, and the list of ways the lab differs from a stock install.

So the gap between disclosed and demonstrated is plain. The record says code execution inside the sandbox. I show a renderer crash on the stock build and the memory error behind it on a sanitizer build.

Detection

The repository ships two rules. Both look for the stylesheet, not for the crash: the XSLT namespace URI, plus an xsl:number whose count or from pattern has two predicates in a row and reads a variable. The Suricata rules match it in an HTTP response body, the YARA rule in a file. There is no Sigma rule, because a stock Chrome leaves only a Crashpad minidump with module offsets, and a renderer crash is not specific to this bug.

The test suite runs 40 checks. Both rules fire once on each of the two live attack captures and stay quiet on the control capture and on a live capture of three ordinary stylesheets rendered by the vulnerable browser. Three things to know before deploying them:

  • They are not quiet on everything benign. Both match 2 of the 1128 stylesheets in DocBook XSL 1.79.2, which number footnotes with a multi-predicate count pattern that reads global parameters. That is the trigger’s shape, used harmlessly.
  • A long attribute can hide the trigger. Each rule has to cover the stretch from the keyword count or from to the two predicates in a single match. The YARA rule stops at 4,096 bytes. For the Suricata rules, with the body in 1400-byte TCP segments, every saved run matched up to 7,500 five-byte union alternatives, about 37.5 kB; above that some runs miss.
  • The network rule needs to see the stylesheet in clear text, so HTTPS needs TLS inspection. And no variation of my own was run against the lab: the variation evidence is the fix commit’s regression stylesheets, for which the evidence holds no lab run, plus the second live capture and synthetic pcaps.

The rules, their tests, the measured limits and the triage steps for a match are in detection/.

The fix

The fix re-reads the slot after the evaluation, so the outer call frees whatever is in the slot now and not what was there before. It is nine added lines in pattern.c.

For users the fix is the update to 157.0.8103.50. Chrome also defines an enterprise policy, XSLTEnabled, whose definition at tag 157.0.8103.38 says that Disabled makes XSLT unavailable. I read the definition and did not test the policy.

Advisory and fix

DateEvent
2026-11-07Fix commit on the release branch, “[M157-mini] Fix use-after-free in libxslt direct pattern match cache”
2026-11-09Stable channel update: Chrome 157.0.8103.50
2026-11-10CVE record published; added to CISA KEV
2026-11-11My reproduction runs (UTC)

The advisory credits the report to Arni Hardarson (Neonix Security) on 2026-10-12 and to an anonymous reporter on 2026-11-06.

Reproduce it

You need a Linux x86_64 host with Docker. From any other machine, add --ssh user@host to the first setup.py command and the lab runs on that host. The first run downloads the pinned Chrome builds and checks each against a sha256.

check.py answers VERDICT: VULNERABLE (confidence: high) for the first target without triggering anything. The first poc.py run ends in RESULT: renderer crash reported by the target in 1/1 rounds -> exit 0, the second, against 157.0.8103.50, in RESULT: no renderer crash in 1/1 rounds -> exit 1. The README lists every step with its expected output, including the sanitizer run and the rule tests, and evidence/INDEX.md lists every evidence file with the command that produced it and the claim it supports.

References

  • CVE record: CVE-2026-125350
  • Fix commit: 049750111b1e, which also adds the crash test xslt-number-pattern-cache-reentrancy-crash.html
  • Vulnerable function: xsltTestCompMatchDirect() at tag 157.0.8103.38
  • XSLTEnabled policy definition: at tag 157.0.8103.38

BTCPay Server is the self-hosted payment processor that Bitcoin merchants use to avoid custodial middlemen. It runs their Lightning nodes, holds their wallet keys, and processes their transactions. Over 30,000 instances run in the wild — on Umbrel boxes, Start9 nodes, bare Docker hosts, and enterprise setups. When BTCPay tells its users to enable two-factor authentication, they trust that the second factor actually matters.

On builds up to 2.4.1, it didn’t. Not on the API.

The Greenfield API — BTCPay’s RESTful interface for everything from store management to Lightning node control — accepts HTTP Basic authentication. The handler that processes Authorization: Basic headers has a single multi-factor gate, and that gate checks for exactly one type of 2FA: FIDO2 hardware keys. If your second factor is a TOTP authenticator app (as it is for the vast majority of users), the handler sees zero FIDO2 credentials, shrugs, and authenticates you with just your password. The browser login page enforces TOTP correctly. The API does not. Two doors to the same house, one locked, one wide open.

This was fixed in v2.4.2 (PR #7491) after being reported by @benthecarman. Attackers exploited it in the wild — Lightning nodes were drained after credentials were stolen. I reproduced it in a local lab to understand what the bypass actually gives an attacker and to ship detection rules.

Repo with PoC, scanner, live PCAP and Suricata/Sigma rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/btcpay-greenfield-2fa-bypass.

What the Greenfield API controls

The Greenfield API is BTCPay Server’s programmatic interface. It manages stores, invoices, wallets, payouts, pull payments, users, server settings, and — critically — Lightning nodes. If you can authenticate to it, you can do everything the web UI does and more. Server-admin accounts get the Unrestricted permission: every endpoint, every store, every node.

The API supports multiple authentication methods: API keys (scoped), Bearer tokens, and HTTP Basic authentication (email + password). Basic auth is the simplest — a single header with base64-encoded credentials — and it’s the one the bypass affects.

The vulnerable code

The authentication decision lives in one file: BasicAuthenticationHandler.cs. Here’s the relevant section from v2.4.1:

user.Fido2Credentials.Any() returns true only for users who registered a hardware security key. A TOTP-only user has zero FIDO2 credentials. The check evaluates to false, the password is verified, and the handler issues a claims identity carrying Unrestricted plus the user’s roles. Two-factor authentication is never consulted.

The browser login path is a completely separate code path. It goes through ASP.NET Identity’s PasswordSignInAsync, which calls IsTwoFactorEnabledAsync and redirects to /login/second-login for the TOTP prompt. The API handler reimplements its own MFA check — and gets it wrong.

The fix in PR #7491 replaces the FIDO2-only test:

IsTwoFactorEnabledAsync checks whether the user has any second factor enabled — TOTP, FIDO2, or future methods. One line, one method call, and the gap is closed.

v2.4.2 also includes PR #7492: Basic auth for the Greenfield API is now disabled by default and only honored for the first 5 minutes after account creation unless a per-user opt-in is set. Defense in depth.

The attack chain

The attack requires a stolen email and password. No TOTP code, no recovery code, no FIDO2 assertion, no API key. Rate limiting is in place, so online brute force is harder — but phished, leaked, or reused credentials are fair game.

Step 1: Send a Basic auth request to any Greenfield endpoint.

The base64 decodes to admin@lab.local:Lab-Passw0rd!2026. No TOTP code anywhere in the request.

Step 2: On BTCPay <= 2.4.1, the server responds with HTTP 200 and the full user identity:

That’s it. Two steps. One HTTP request. The attacker is now authenticated as a server admin with unrestricted API access.

The proof

I set up a lab with PostgreSQL, BTCPay 2.4.1 (vulnerable), and BTCPay 2.4.2 (fixed). On each I provisioned an admin account with real TOTP 2FA enabled through the actual web enrollment flow — not a mock, not a database hack, but the same process a real user follows. The database confirmed TwoFactorEnabled=true, an AuthenticatorKey token stored, and zero FIDO2 credentials. The exact vulnerable precondition.

The /api/v1/users endpoint lists every account on the server — a server-admin-only endpoint. It returns HTTP 200. The Lightning endpoint returns 404 because I didn’t configure a node in the minimal lab, but the response is 404 (lightning-not-configured), not 401 or 403 — authentication passed; the failure is at the resource level. The endpoint is reachable past the auth gate.

The verify dashboard ran 5 rounds at 100%:

Negative control

The identical request against patched v2.4.2:

The fix works. The rejection message is the exact string introduced in PR #7491.

Honest impact assessment

I want to be specific about what I proved and what I didn’t.

The bypass gives an attacker with stolen credentials full Unrestricted Greenfield API access. For a server-admin account, that means every endpoint on the server. I confirmed this by reaching the server-admin-only /api/v1/users endpoint (lists all accounts) via the bypass.

The Lightning endpoints are reachable past authentication. In the wild, attackers reportedly used this to extract LND macaroons and drain channels. I did not configure a Lightning node in my lab, so I did not extract a macaroon or move funds. The README claims table marks this as “Not proven” — the endpoint is reachable (auth passes), but the consequential step of credential extraction and fund movement was not exercised.

ClaimStatus
TOTP bypass via Basic authProven
Server-admin API accessProven
Lightning endpoint reachabilityProven (auth passes, 404 = not configured)
Macaroon extraction / fund theftNot proven (not exercised)
Patched v2.4.2 blocks the bypassConfirmed

Detection

I wrote Suricata and Sigma rules to detect exploitation. The Suricata rules (SIDs 9100001–9100003) fire on HTTP Basic auth to Greenfield API paths, with elevated severity for server-admin and Lightning endpoints. I validated them against the live PCAP using jasonish/suricata — all rules fire correctly.

The Sigma rules target reverse-proxy access logs (BTCPay’s own app log doesn’t record Greenfield auth decisions at default verbosity — I checked). The rules include the nginx log_format directive needed to capture the Authorization scheme.

Both rule sets and the PCAP are in the repo.

The fix

Upgrade to BTCPay Server 2.4.2 or later. The upgrade also requires NBXplorer 2.6.10.

Patching alone is not enough if credentials were already stolen. BTCPay’s own advisory was explicit about this: rotate LND macaroons, CLN runes, and any API keys that may have been exposed. The bypass let attackers extract credentials that survive a software update.

For defense in depth: use scoped API keys instead of Basic auth for all Greenfield integrations. v2.4.2 disables Basic auth by default for established accounts (PR #7492), but the opt-in exists and some workflows may re-enable it.

Timeline

DateEvent
2026-08-04PR #7491 merged (fix by NicolasDorier, reported by benthecarman)
2026-08-07BTCPay Server v2.4.2 released
2026-08-08Media reports of Lightning node draining via stolen credentials
2026-11-04This write-up published

No CVE ID or GitHub Security Advisory was published by the vendor.

Reproduction

Every claim in this post can be verified by running these commands. The scripts use only Python stdlib.

Langflow is an open-source visual framework for building LLM-powered applications. It has over 55k stars on GitHub, ships as a Docker image, and lands in production faster than most teams can audit it. When its agentic assistant generates a Python component, a security scanner walks the AST looking for dangerous imports — os, subprocess, ctypes, shutil, and 30-odd others. The scanner blocks them all. It does not block pydoc.

That is CVE-2026-110186 in one import statement. pydoc is part of the Python standard library. It generates documentation. And it re-exports the os module as pydoc.os. One import pydoc passes the scanner, and pydoc.os.popen(cmd) gives you a shell on the Langflow server. With LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true — the default — the entire chain is unauthenticated. CVSS 9.8.

Repo with PoC, scanner, Suricata/Sigma detection rules, and PCAP: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-110186.

What Langflow is, and why it has a code scanner

Langflow lets you drag components onto a canvas, wire them together, and produce an LLM-backed application. Think of it as a visual pipeline editor for AI workflows. Components are Python classes that inherit from Component and define inputs, outputs, and a build_output() method.

The agentic assistant takes this further: you describe what you want in natural language, and the assistant generates the component code for you. Because LLMs can write anything — including os.system("rm -rf /") — Langflow runs the generated code through scan_code_security() in code_security.py before it reaches the Python interpreter. This is the gate between “LLM-generated text” and “code running on your server.”

The scanner is AST-based. It parses the code, walks the tree, and rejects anything that imports from a blocklist. The blocklist is thorough: os, subprocess, sys, ctypes, shutil, socket, importlib, multiprocessing, signal, and many more. If the LLM generates import os, the scanner catches it. If it generates from subprocess import Popen, the scanner catches it. Even __import__("os") is blocked.

But Python’s standard library is vast, and modules reference each other in ways that no blocklist can fully enumerate.

The vulnerable code

Here is the relevant part of code_security.py in Langflow 1.12.5 (simplified):

Notice what is not in the list: pydoc.

Now look at what pydoc gives you:

pydoc imports os at module level and exposes it as an attribute. pydoc.os is the real os module — not a wrapper, not a subset, the actual module object. Every function in os is accessible through it: popen, system, execve, listdir, remove. The scanner sees import pydoc and shrugs. It never checks what pydoc re-exports.

The same class of bypass exists in numpy.ctypeslib, which re-exports ctypes for native library loading. Both were blocked in PR #15586.

The attack chain

With LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true — which is Langflow’s default — the entire exploit requires zero credentials:

Step 1: Get a superuser JWT.

The server hands back an access_token with full superuser privileges. No username, no password. This is by design — Langflow’s auto-login mode is intended for development.

Step 2: Create an API key.

The API key is needed to authenticate the flow execution endpoint.

Step 3: Get the CustomComponent template.

This returns every component type, including CustomComponent — the template for user-defined components. I need its exact structure to create a valid flow.

Step 4: Create a flow with the pydoc bypass.

The flow contains a single custom component:

import pydoc passes the scanner. pydoc.os is not flagged because the scanner only checks the import itself, not attribute access on allowed modules. The variable assignment _os = pydoc.os gives us full os module access under a clean alias.

Step 5: Run the flow.

The server imports the component, calls build_output(), and the command executes.

The proof

The server process runs as uid=1000(user) gid=0(root) groups=0(root). The Langflow Docker image runs as a non-root user, but the user belongs to the root group. The command output is written to a marker file on the server, proving server-side execution.

The non-destructive scanner confirms the same target without triggering the vulnerability:

The negative control (and a surprise)

I expected Langflow 1.12.6 — the version with the fix backported — to block the exploit. It does not.

PR #15586 adds pydoc to DANGEROUS_IMPORTS in code_security.py. I verified the fix is present in the 1.12.6 Docker image — grep -n "pydoc" code_security.py finds it at line 295. But the scanner only guards the agentic assistant code generation path. My exploit uses the standard flow REST API (POST /api/v1/flows/ → POST /api/v1/run/), which executes custom component code without passing through code_security.py at all.

The scan_code_security() function is called from assistant_service.py, user_components.py, user_components_overlay.py, and flow_run.py — all agentic paths. The standard flow API is a separate execution path with no code validation gate.

This means the pydoc bypass is fixed for the agentic assistant, but the broader attack surface — arbitrary code execution through the flow API — remains open in 1.12.6. The flow API trusts that the code it receives has already been validated, but there is no validation on this path.

Impact

An attacker with network access to a Langflow instance can execute arbitrary commands as the Langflow process user. With the default LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=true configuration, no credentials are needed. The attack requires five HTTP requests and takes under one second.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Code injection via pydoc bypassProvenpydoc.os.popen() executes on target
Unauthenticated RCE (default config)ProvenFull chain, zero credentials
Flow API lacks code validationProvenExploit succeeds on 1.12.6 despite fix
PR #15586 blocks agentic pathConfirmedpydoc present in 1.12.6 DANGEROUS_IMPORTS

Detection

I wrote Suricata and Sigma rules to detect exploitation. The Suricata rules match the three key API endpoints: GET /api/v1/auto_login, POST /api/v1/flows/ with pydoc in the body, and POST /api/v1/run/. The Sigma rule covers the same patterns in web server access logs.

Both rule sets are in the detection/ directory. The capture/ directory has a 24-packet PCAP of the full exploit chain, with no TLS, so the payload is visible to any inline IDS:

The fix

PR #15586 adds two entries:

And adds ("numpy", "ctypeslib", ...) to DANGEROUS_ATTRIBUTE_READS, blocking numpy.ctypeslib access at the AST level.

The fix is correct for the agentic assistant path: import pydoc is now rejected before the code reaches the interpreter. The broader question of whether the flow API should also validate component code is a design decision that goes beyond this CVE.

Affected versions: 1.9.0 through 1.12.5 (on the agentic path). Fix backported in 1.12.6, included in 1.13.0.

Timeline

DateEvent
2026Vulnerability discovered and reported
2026PR #15586 merged (fix)
2026Langflow 1.12.6 released with backport
2026Langflow 1.13.0 released
2026-11-04This write-up published

Reproduction

Every claim in this post can be verified by running these commands against the lab environment. The scripts use only Python stdlib — no pip dependencies.
