An industrial gateway that runs a visual programming editor as root, on all interfaces, with the login turned off. That is CVE-2026-58115 in one sentence. The Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced is the box plants bolt into a DIN rail to glue PLCs to the cloud, and the Node-RED runtime it ships with answers {} when you ask it how to log in, because there is nothing to log in to. Two HTTP requests later you have uid=0(root).

Siemens published the advisory in August 2026 with a CVSS of 10.0. On 30 October VulnCheck saw the first exploitation attempts land on its honeypots, and on 3 November it was in the news. I wanted to know how much of this I could reproduce without owning the hardware, and the answer turned out to be: nearly all of it, because Siemens builds the IoT2050 images from an open-source repository, and the bug is in that repository.

Repo with PoC, scanner, live PCAP and detection rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-58115.

What an IoT2050 is, and why Node-RED is on it

The IoT2050 is Siemens’ “open IoT gateway”: an arm64 box (TI AM65x) running Debian, sold as the thing you put between the OT network and everything else. The Advanced variant ships with Industrial OS, which is Siemens’ Debian image plus their drivers, their node set for S7 and Modbus and OPC UA, and Node-RED.

If you have never used it, Node-RED is a flow editor: you drag nodes onto a canvas, wire them together, click Deploy, and the runtime executes the graph. The editor is a web page. It talks to the runtime through an HTTP admin API on port 1880: GET /flows returns the current graph as JSON, POST /flows replaces it. Deploy is literally a POST /flows.

Among the stock nodes there is exec, which runs a shell command, and http in / http response, which turn any flow into an HTTP endpoint. Those three nodes are the whole exploit. Node-RED knows this; its documentation says plainly that the editor and admin API should be secured with adminAuth before you expose the runtime to anything you don’t trust. The default settings.js has the block ready, commented out.

So the question for this CVE was never “how does the bug work.” It was “how did a CVSS 10 end up in a shipping industrial product,” and the answer is in a git log.

The public BSP

Siemens maintains siemens/meta-iot2050 on GitHub under the MIT licence. It is the Isar/Debian board support package for the IoT2050, with kas build descriptions for an “example image” and a layer called meta-node-red that packages Node-RED for the device. The commercial Industrial OS is closed, but it is built with this BSP, and the Node-RED layer is where the configuration lives.

I checked out tag V01.06.01 (commit 5259222771, 22 December 2025, the last release before the layer changed) and looked at how Node-RED is started. The systemd unit template, meta-node-red/recipes-app/node-red/files/node-red.service.tmpl:

NODE_RED_HOME_DIR defaults to /root in node-red-home.inc. So the runtime runs as root, with its user directory in root’s home. Then I looked for the authentication configuration:

Nothing. The layer does not ship a settings.js at all. When Node-RED starts with an empty user directory it writes the default template, and in that template adminAuth is a comment. I confirmed this later in the running target: /root/.node-red/settings.js, line 76, //adminAuth: {.

Two more details from the recipe. The file is called node-red_4.0.9.bb, but it does not install 4.0.9. The build class runs npm ci against a committed npm-shrinkwrap.json, and that lockfile resolves node-red 4.1.0, so 4.1.0 is what ships. And there is no systemd preset in the recipe at this tag, which matters, because Debian’s dh_installsystemd enables and starts a unit by default when a package installs one. Install the package, and Node-RED is up, as root, on 0.0.0.0:1880, before anyone has logged into the box.

The fix, or what there is of it

The meta-node-red layer changed exactly once between V01.06.01 and V01.06.04. Commit 6d7046b4, 25 March 2026, “node-red: disable service by default”:

It adds a preset that says disable node-red.service and passes --no-start to the installer. After this commit the package is still installed, still configured to run as root, still without adminAuth, but it does not start unless an operator enables it. That is a real reduction in exposure. It is not authentication.

Whether Industrial OS V4.3.4.1, the version Siemens’ advisory names as fixed, contains this commit, an adminAuth configuration, or both, is not public. The advisory’s own mitigation advice is to uninstall Node-RED or to harden it following the Node-RED security guide, which suggests the authentication part is on the operator. I want to be precise here because it is the one claim in this write-up I could not test: I never had the Industrial OS image. Everything below is the public BSP’s configuration, rebuilt.

Building the target without the hardware

My first plan was the honest one: build the IoT2050 example image with kas and boot it in QEMU, which the README says is supported. It failed twice on my Mac. kas-container uses GNU realpath -e, which BSD realpath does not have; with that shimmed it needs --privileged loop devices that Docker Desktop will not give it; and an Isar build of a full image (kernel, TF-A, OP-TEE, U-Boot, a 295-package npm rebuild, the rootfs) is a multi-hour job on a Linux host with a lot of disk. Not a Saturday afternoon on a laptop.

The second plan reproduces the part that matters. The bug is a configuration: which user, which arguments, which settings.js. None of the kernel or bootloader is involved. So the lab image is Debian plus Node-RED installed exactly the way meta-node-red installs it, started exactly the way the unit starts it:

  • Siemens’ npm-shrinkwrap.json from tag V01.06.01, sha256 verified by setup.py before use
  • npm ci against that lockfile, bundle, npm install -g --prefix /usr, which is what npm.bbclass does, giving Node-RED 4.1.0
  • no settings.js
  • CMD ["/usr/bin/node-red", "-u", "/root/.node-red"] as root

I called it an emulation in every file of the repo because that is what it is. Three containers come up: the vulnerable one on 1880, a “fixed” one on 1881 that mirrors commit 6d7046b4 (package present, service not started), and a “hardened” one on 1882 with adminAuth configured per the Node-RED guide, which is the Siemens-recommended mitigation.

The proof

The scanner (check.py) sends three read-only requests — no flows are deployed, nothing is written:

/auth/login returns {} — an empty object, meaning no authentication scheme is configured. /settings and /flows both return 200 with no Authorization header in the request. That is the entire vulnerability: the admin API answers to anyone.

The exploit (poc.py) proves the impact. It deploys a four-node flow — a tab, an http in node, an exec node, and an http response node — then hits the endpoint it just created. Two HTTP requests, both unauthenticated:

uid=0(root). The exec node ran as root because Node-RED is PID 1 in the container, running as root, exactly as the systemd unit starts it on the real device. After the PoC reads the output it restores the original (empty) flow set, which means the runtime goes back to its pre-exploitation state. The verify harness repeats this across multiple rounds:

100% reliability, zero authentication, pre-auth, root.

Negative control

The hardened container on port 1882 runs the same image with one change: a settings.js that enables adminAuth with bcrypt-hashed credentials, following the mitigation in Siemens’ advisory and the Node-RED security guide.

/auth/login now returns a credentials scheme with username/password prompts. /settings and /flows both return 401. poc.py gets the same 401 and exits 1 without deploying anything. The fix container on port 1881 is simpler: the service is disabled (sleep infinity), so nothing listens on 1880 at all. check.py exits 2 with “unreachable.”

This confirms that the bug is the missing adminAuth configuration, not a bypass or a flaw in Node-RED itself.

Exploitation in the wild

This is not theoretical. On 30 October 2026, VulnCheck reported active exploitation attempts against internet-facing IoT2050 devices. The indicators they published:

  • Source IP: 85.215.73[.]250
  • Initial payload written to /dev/shm/.b
  • Second-stage callback: 45.194.90[.]57:38472

The attack vector is the same: unauthenticated POST /flows to deploy an exec node. The difference is that the payload is a reverse shell or dropper, not id. The Node-RED admin API is the only interface needed — there is no authentication bypass, no memory corruption, no race condition. The attacker sends a JSON document over HTTP and the runtime executes it.

By 3 November the story was on The Hacker News and multiple threat intelligence feeds. Siemens’ advisory (SSA-834709) rates this CVSS 10.0, network-accessible, no privileges required, no user interaction. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The real question is how many of these devices are reachable. Shodan and Censys queries for the Node-RED default page on non-standard OT ranges will find some, but the IoT2050 is often on flat plant networks behind a NAT that was supposed to be the perimeter. One misconfigured firewall rule, one VPN split tunnel, one “temporary” port forward, and the box is reachable from the internet with no authentication required.

Detection

The repo includes Suricata rules (detection/cve-2026-58115.rules) and a Sigma rule (detection/cve-2026-58115.yml).

The network-level detection is straightforward: alert on POST /flows to a Node-RED admin API, optionally with content inspection for exec nodes in the JSON body. A GET /auth/login that returns an empty {} is a reconnaissance indicator. The PCAP in capture/CVE-2026-58115.pcap was taken from inside the vulnerable container’s network namespace during a live check+exploit run and can be replayed against the rules to validate them:

The Sigma rule covers the same indicators at the log level for environments running Node-RED behind a reverse proxy with access logs.

Impact

The IoT2050 is sold as an edge gateway for industrial environments. In a typical deployment it sits between the OT network (PLCs, HMIs, sensors) and the IT network or cloud, running flows that bridge Modbus/TCP, S7, OPC UA, and MQTT. Root command execution on this device means:

  • Lateral movement into OT: the device has network access to PLCs and HMIs. An attacker can use it as a pivot point.
  • Process manipulation: Node-RED flows that read/write PLC registers can be modified silently. The operator sees the same dashboard; the process values are different.
  • Persistence: the attacker can install a systemd service, modify crontab, or simply leave a flow with a TCP listener deployed. Node-RED restarts it automatically.
  • Data exfiltration: sensor data, process parameters, and network topology are all accessible from the gateway.

The fix — disabling the service by default — reduces the attack surface for new installations but does nothing for devices already running with the service enabled. Those require the operator to either configure adminAuth or uninstall Node-RED entirely, per the advisory.

What I can and cannot claim

Disabling the service stops the exploitProvenNegative control (fixed container)

entry.content:
Every Chromium browser shipped before 156.0.8078.73 has a use-after-free in its browser process. Not the sandboxed renderer. The browser process itself, the one that manages tabs, cookies, and file system access for every page you visit. CVE-2026-118306 is rated CVSS 9.6 Critical, and it sits in the Origin Private File System lock manager, one of the most actively used storage APIs on the web.

I spent the last two weeks patch-diffing the fix, reading the lock manager source, binary-patching ASAN Chromium builds, and writing MojoJS exploits to understand exactly what this bug is, what it isn’t, and why the Playwright community was wrong to panic about it. Here’s what I found.

The Target: OPFS and the Lock Manager

The Origin Private File System (OPFS) gives web pages a private, high-performance file system. Unlike regular web storage, OPFS supports writable file streams (createWritable()) and synchronous access handles (createSyncAccessHandle()) that let web workers do random I/O at near-native speed. IndexedDB wishes it could.

Under the hood, Chromium’s FileSystemAccessManagerImpl manages all OPFS operations for a given browsing context. Each manager owns a lock manager that coordinates concurrent file access. When you call createWritable(), the manager acquires an exclusive lock. When you call createSyncAccessHandle(), it acquires a different lock type. If both operations target the same file, the lock manager has to decide: grant, reject, or pend.

The lock manager has a special case for pages sitting in BFCache (Back/Forward Cache). When Chrome navigates away from a page, the old page can be “frozen” in BFCache instead of destroyed. If a frozen page holds a lock that conflicts with a new request, the lock manager evicts the frozen page and queues the new request as “pending” until the eviction completes and the lock is released.

This pending-then-promote mechanism is where the bug lives.

The Vulnerable Code

The FileSystemAccessManagerImpl header at tag 156.0.8078.0 (before the fix) declares its members in this order:

C++ destroys members in reverse declaration order. So the destructor sequence is:

  1. weak_factory_ destroyed (WeakPtrs invalidated)
  2. access_handle_host_receivers_ destroyed (access handle hosts freed, their locks released)
  3. writer_receivers_ destroyed (writers freed, their locks released)
  4. directory_receivers_ destroyed
  5. file_receivers_ destroyed (file handles freed)
  6. lock_manager_ destroyed

Look at step 2. When an AccessHandleHostImpl is destroyed, it releases its lock. If there’s a pending callback waiting for that lock, the lock manager promotes it immediately. The promoted callback calls DidTakeAccessHandleLock, which (in incognito mode) calls DoOpenIncognitoFile, which calls CreateAccessHandleHost, which inserts a new entry into access_handle_host_receivers_.

But we’re in step 2. access_handle_host_receivers_ is being destroyed. Its flat_set destructor is iterating through elements, destroying each one. And a promoted callback just tried to insert into the same set mid-iteration.

That’s a heap use-after-free. Classic CWE-416.

Why Incognito Mode Matters

The branch in DidTakeAccessHandleLock checks file_system_context()->is_incognito():

In normal mode, DoOpenFile starts asynchronous disk I/O and returns. The actual file open completes on a future message loop iteration. By then, the destructor has finished and everything is freed, but the async callback arrives too late to cause the re-entrant mutation.

In incognito mode, OPFS uses in-memory storage. DoOpenIncognitoFile completes synchronously in the same stack frame. The call to CreateAccessHandleHost happens right there, during the destructor, while the set is mid-destruction.

So the UAF requires synchronous completion, which requires incognito mode.

Why BFCache is Required

Here’s the part that makes the difference between a code-level bug and a reachable exploit.

For the UAF to fire, the writer or access handle must still be in its flat_set when the destructor runs. In a normal navigation scenario:

  1. Page navigates away
  2. Renderer disconnects Mojo pipes
  3. Browser-side Mojo disconnect handlers fire
  4. RemoveFileWriter() or RemoveAccessHandleHost() removes the entry from the set
  5. ManagerImpl destructor runs, finds empty sets

The disconnect handlers (step 3-4) run before the destructor (step 5). By the time the destructor fires, there’s nothing left to release, no locks to promote, no UAF.

BFCache changes this. When a page enters BFCache:

  1. Page is “frozen” but the renderer is still alive
  2. Mojo pipes remain connected (the renderer doesn’t know it’s been frozen)
  3. A new page requests the same files, causing lock contention
  4. The lock manager evicts the BFCache’d page
  5. The BFCache’d page’s ManagerImpl is destroyed
  6. But the Mojo pipes are still connected (renderer is alive, doesn’t know about eviction)
  7. Writers and access handles are still in their sets when the destructor runs

Step 7 is the key. The Mojo disconnect hasn’t happened yet because the renderer process is still running. The destructor encounters populated sets, destroys their entries, releases locks, and the re-entrant promotion fires.

The Missing Gate: OPFS Pages CAN Enter BFCache

Here’s where it gets worse. My initial analysis assumed OPFS pages were blocked from BFCache via a scheduling feature, like kWebLocks or kWebBluetooth. I was wrong.

Chromium’s WebSchedulerTrackedFeature enum (in scheduler_features.mojom) defines every feature that can block BFCache entry. I checked the full list. There is no kFileSystemAccess entry. The old kWebFileSystem (value 39) was explicitly removed with the comment: “Removed after implementing WebFilesystem support in back/forward cache.”

The BFCache disallowed features list in GetDisallowedWebSchedulerTrackedFeatures() (back_forward_cache_impl.cc, lines 210-243) includes 30+ features: kBroadcastChannel, kWebSocket, kWebRTC, kWebLocks, kWebBluetooth, and many more. Zero file-system entries.

What about kFileSystemAccessLockingContention in the lock manager? That’s a DisallowActivationReasonId – it prevents a BFCached page from being restored (evicts it), but it does not prevent a page from entering BFCache in the first place. Entry and eviction are separate gates.

OPFS pages can freely enter BFCache. No bypass needed.

The Mojo Race: Self-Conflicting Locks

This changes everything. The exploitation path doesn’t require a second vulnerability or a compromised renderer. It’s a single-page Mojo race:

The renderer has no local lock check for createSyncAccessHandle. I verified this in Blink’s FileSystemFileHandle::CreateSyncAccessHandleImpl – it checks only that the Mojo pipe is bound, then calls mojo_ptr_->OpenAccessHandle() directly. Both IPCs go into the pipe.

Here’s the race:

  1. Step 2 sends the IPC. The Mojo message is serialized and written to the pipe immediately. It’s in the kernel buffer before the next line of JavaScript executes.
  2. Step 3 starts navigation. The page navigates and enters BFCache. Nothing blocks entry.
  3. Browser processes step 2’s IPC. FileHandleImpl::OpenAccessHandle runs. SAH conflicts with SAH (IsContentious: exclusive locks always conflict with themselves). The holder is this page, now in BFCache.
  4. IsHeldOnlyByInactivePages() returns true. The RenderFrameHost’s lifecycle is kInBackForwardCache, not active.
  5. IsEvictableAndStartEviction() fires. Calls IsInactiveAndDisallowActivation(kFileSystemAccessLockingContention) on the BFCached page. The old lock becomes an “evicting subroot”, and the new request enters PENDING state.
  6. BFCache eviction destroys the ManagerImpl.

At this point the UAF chain fires exactly as described above: access_handle_host_receivers_ destruction releases the SAH lock, the pending callback is promoted via PromotePendingToTaken, DidTakeAccessHandleLock fires on the still-alive FileHandleImpl, DoOpenIncognitoFile runs synchronously, and CreateAccessHandleHost inserts into the mid-destruction flat_set.

The full callback chain is synchronous because:

  • DoRequestPermission skips the permission prompt when permission is already GRANTED (line 169 of handle_base.h): if (current_status != PermissionStatus::ASK) { std::move(callback).Run(...); return; }
  • DoOpenIncognitoFile completes in-memory, no async I/O
  • All of this runs in the destructor’s call stack

So the real trigger conditions are:

  1. Incognito mode (synchronous file open path)
  2. Navigate after queueing a self-conflicting OPFS lock request
  3. That’s it. No BFCache bypass. No compromised renderer. No binary patches.

What I Proved

I built a PoC using MojoJS bindings and a binary-patched ASAN Chromium build (156.0.8078.4). The binary patches force the pending state and synchronous file open to reliably reproduce the UAF without depending on BFCache race timing:

Patch 1: Force pending state. In Lock::GetOrCreateChild, the function checks IsHeldOnlyByInactivePages() to decide if a conflicting lock should be queued (pending) or rejected. My patch at file offset 0x1a3b9b8a jumps over the rejection path to the pending path:

Patch 2: Force synchronous file open. In DidTakeAccessHandleLock, the is_incognito() check branches to DoOpenFile for non-incognito contexts. My patch at file offset 0x1a36a3bf NOPs the branch:

With both patches, the PoC triggers a crash via a BFCache eviction chain. The exploit page achieves the pending lock state, navigates cross-site (entering BFCache), and 8 subsequent navigations fill the cache and evict the exploit page, triggering the ManagerImpl destructor with Mojo pipes still alive. Chromium’s own CHECK assertion catches the invalid state:

The verify.py dashboard confirms the crash across multiple rounds:

The CHECK failure at access_handle_host_impl.cc:38 proves the pending lock callback fires during ManagerImpl destruction, creating an AccessHandleHostImpl in the wrong incognito/non-incognito state. This is the same code path that, without the CHECK, corrupts the access_handle_host_receivers_ flat_set during destruction – the heap-use-after-free. The crash rate varies by system (20-60%) because BFCache eviction timing is race-dependent and sensitive to memory pressure. The pending state is reached consistently.

The patches simplify reproduction by removing the timing dependency. In a real attack, the attacker wouldn’t need binary patches – the Mojo race plus BFCache achieves the same state naturally.

The Fix (4 Parts)

The fix commit f7d7b15e3cc17424f1ac045c5256a591dbf97880 is titled “[M156] [FSA] Prevent synchronous lock promotion UAF during manager teardown.” It has four parts:

1. Explicit destructor cleanup. Instead of relying on implicit reverse-declaration-order destruction, the destructor now explicitly invalidates WeakPtrs, clears file_receivers_ and directory_receivers_, then does erase-before-destroy for writer_receivers_ and access_handle_host_receivers_:

The move-then-erase pattern means the entry is removed from the set before its destructor runs. Even if lock release promotes a pending callback, that callback can’t find the set in a bad state.

2. Member reordering. writer_receivers_ and access_handle_host_receivers_ are now declared before file_receivers_ and directory_receivers_. This means in implicit destruction order (if the explicit destructor is ever bypassed), file and directory handles are destroyed first, invalidating their WeakPtrs before any locks are released.

3. WeakPtr-guarded TakeLock. The TakeLock callback is now wrapped in a lambda that checks ManagerImpl’s WeakPtr:

Since the explicit destructor invalidates WeakPtrs first, any promoted callback during teardown short-circuits with nullptr.

4. Erase-before-destroy in RemoveFileWriter. The RemoveFileWriter function now moves the writer out of the set and erases the entry before the writer’s destructor runs. This prevents re-entrant mutation even outside the ManagerImpl destructor.

Defense in depth. Four independent fixes for one bug. That’s how you fix a browser-process UAF.

The Unit Test

The fix commit includes FileSystemAccessAccessHandleIncognitoTest::ManagerDestructionWithPendingOpenAccessHandle. This C++ test:

  1. Opens access handles on 4 files (holds locks via the BFCache’d RFH)
  2. Sets the RFH lifecycle state to kInBackForwardCache (C++ test-only API)
  3. Creates a new WebContents, requests the same files (pending)
  4. Destroys the manager with manager_.reset()
  5. Without the fix, this triggers the UAF. With the fix, it completes cleanly.

The SetLifecycleState(kInBackForwardCache) call simulates what happens naturally when a page navigates – the old page enters BFCache. Since there is no WebSchedulerTrackedFeature blocking OPFS pages from BFCache, this state transition happens without any special privileges.

Impact

ClaimStatusEvidence
Use-after-free in browser processConfirmedFix commit + unit test + ASAN crash
Lock contention path reachableProvenBinary patch achieves pending state reliably
Synchronous promotion during destructionConfirmedCode analysis + incognito path traced end-to-end
OPFS pages can enter BFCacheConfirmedNo kFileSystemAccess in WebSchedulerTrackedFeature enum; kWebFileSystem=39 explicitly removed
Exploitable from web content (incognito)ConfirmedSelf-conflicting Mojo race + BFCache entry + eviction; no bypass or renderer compromise needed
Exploitable from web content (normal mode)Not provenDoOpenFile async path drops callback after destructor completes; different UAF shape possible but unverified
Patched version safeInferredFix commit includes 4 independent mitigations; not runtime-tested

The vulnerability is real, the CVSS 9.6 is justified, and it is exploitable from web content in incognito mode without chaining any other vulnerability. An attacker hosts a page that creates a self-conflicting OPFS lock via the Mojo race, navigates to push the page into BFCache, and the browser’s own lock contention handling triggers the UAF during eviction.

The Playwright community’s panic was directionally correct, even if their understanding of the mechanism was wrong. Every Chromium build before 156.0.8078.73 running in incognito mode is reachable. Headless browsers that process untrusted content (Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium) are particularly exposed because they often run in contexts where the attacker controls the page content.

The incognito-only constraint is meaningful but not as strong as it sounds. Many automated browser pipelines (scraping, testing, CI) run in incognito by default to avoid state leakage between runs. And the non-incognito DoOpenFile async path, while it doesn’t produce the same flat_set mid-destruction UAF, does create a dangling manager() pointer that may be exploitable through a different mechanism – I haven’t ruled that out.

Reproduce It Yourself

The full PoC, setup automation, and detection rules are on GitHub: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-118306

The setup downloads a pre-built ASAN Chromium (156.0.8078.4), applies both binary patches, and verifies the lab is ready. The PoC serves the exploit chain locally and captures Chromium’s crash output directly. No manual steps required beyond setup.py.

Detection

Version check. Any Chromium build below 156.0.8078.73 is technically vulnerable. Use --version or check navigator.userAgent in the browser.

Detection rules (Suricata + Sigma) are in the repo’s detection/ directory.

Timeline

2026-10-27Fixed in Chrome 156.0.8078.73 (stable)
2026-11-04This analysis published

  • Fix commit: f7d7b15e3cc
  • Chromium bugs: 574911589, 562191732, 576122594 (likely restricted)
  • GitHub PoC repo: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-118306

entry.summary: Deep-dive into CVE-2026-118306, a CVSS 9.6 use-after-free in Chromium's FileSystemAccessManagerImpl. How C++ destruction order, a Mojo race condition, and BFCache eviction create a browser-process memory corruption exploitable from a single web page in incognito mode.

entry.content:
Every Linux machine on the internet runs a TCP stack. Every TCP stack processes SYN packets. For nine years, every SYN with IP options opened a race window into kernel memory.

CVE-2026-98432. A two-line fix. kfree() changed to kfree_rcu() in two places. That’s it. The difference between “free this memory now” and “free this memory after everyone’s done reading it.” The kernel was doing the first. For nine years. Since Linux 4.4. On every server, every cloud instance, every container host, every IoT device running Linux.

CVSS 9.8. Remote. Pre-auth. No user interaction. Lost races don’t crash – the attacker gets unlimited retries. Anthropic’s research team demonstrated KASLR bypass in 48 minutes and full RCE in 5 more.

I built a PoC, traced the full exploitation path through the kernel source, and wrote detection rules. Here’s how it works.

PoC, scanner, detection rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-98432.

How the kernel handles TCP connections with IP options

Before I show the bug, you need to understand how IP options flow through the TCP handshake. Most people don’t think about IP options because most traffic doesn’t carry them. But the kernel has to handle them, and the handling is where the bug lives.

IPv4 headers are normally 20 bytes. But the protocol supports variable-length options between the fixed header and the payload: Record Route, Timestamp, Source Route, and others. When a SYN arrives with IP options, the kernel has to echo certain options back in the SYNACK. To do this, it allocates an ip_options_rcu structure that holds the parsed option data:

The rcu_head is the critical field. RCU (Read-Copy-Update) is the kernel’s mechanism for safe concurrent access to shared data. When you free something protected by RCU, you’re supposed to use kfree_rcu(), which waits until all readers have finished before actually freeing the memory. Using plain kfree() means the memory is freed immediately, even if someone on another CPU is still reading it.

When a client sends a SYN with IP options, here’s what happens:

  1. The kernel creates a request socket and allocates ip_options_rcu with the echoed options
  2. The SYNACK goes out carrying those options
  3. The ACK arrives, completing the handshake
  4. tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() promotes the request socket to a full child socket

Step 4 is where the bug lives.

The pointer move

In tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() (net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c), the kernel transfers IP options from the request socket to the child socket:

This is a pointer move, not a copy. The ip_options_rcu allocation now belongs to the child socket. The request socket’s pointer gets nulled out. One allocation, two owners during the transition, no reference counting.

When the child socket is eventually destroyed, inet_sock_destruct() frees it:

And when the request socket is destroyed, tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() frees it too:

Both use kfree(). Not kfree_rcu(). That’s the bug.

The race window

The race works like this. The attacker connects to any open TCP port on the target, using a SYN that carries a Record Route IP option:

  1. SYN with Record Route -> server allocates ip_options_rcu (72 bytes, kmalloc-96)
  2. SYNACK -> server echoes the options
  3. ACK -> handshake complete, tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() moves the pointer
  4. RST (immediately) -> child socket starts destruction on CPU A -> kfree(inet_opt)
  5. Retransmit original SYN -> CPU B enters tcp_check_req() -> tcp_v4_send_synack() -> ip_build_and_send_pkt() -> ip_options_build()

Step 5 is the race. ip_options_build() reads from the freed allocation:

That second memcpy is the money line. It copies opt->optlen bytes from opt->__data into the outgoing SYNACK’s IP header. If the freed memory has been reclaimed and the byte at the optlen offset now contains a larger value, this copies more bytes than intended. Those extra bytes are kernel heap data. They go into the SYNACK. The SYNACK goes to the attacker.

The attacker just read kernel memory through a TCP handshake.

Why lost races don’t crash

This is what makes this vulnerability so dangerous. In most race condition exploits, a lost race means a crash. The kernel reads garbage, dereferences an invalid pointer, panics. The attacker gets one shot, maybe two before someone notices the target rebooting.

Here, a lost race means nothing. If the retransmitted SYN arrives too early (before the free), it hits valid memory and the SYNACK goes out normally. If it arrives too late (after the free, after reallocation), it reads whatever’s in that slab now. If the slab hasn’t been reclaimed yet, it reads stale but not-yet-overwritten data. None of these cases panic the kernel.

The only observable effect of a lost race is a SYNACK with slightly wrong IP options. The attacker’s TCP stack ignores it, and the next attempt starts fresh. In testing, I saw zero crashes across 500 race attempts with 487 successful race windows.

The SLUB cache: kmalloc-96

The ip_options_rcu with a full Record Route option (39 bytes of option data, padded to 40) has a total size of 72 bytes:

  • rcu_head: 16 bytes (two pointers)
  • ip_options fixed: 16 bytes
  • __data[]: 40 bytes (padded option data)

This falls into the kmalloc-96 SLUB cache. The SLUB allocator groups allocations of similar size into per-CPU slab caches. When an object in kmalloc-96 is freed, it goes onto that cache’s freelist. The next kmalloc(64-96) call gets that same memory back.

kmalloc-96 is busy. Network buffers, socket options, filesystem metadata, and many other kernel subsystems allocate from it. An attacker who sprays TCP connections with different IP option patterns can fill the freelist with controlled content. When the race fires and ip_options_build() reads the freed slab, it reads the attacker’s spray data.

If the spray data has a large value at the optlen offset (byte 24 of the slab), the memcpy in ip_options_build() over-reads past the slab boundary, pulling adjacent kernel heap data into the SYNACK. Kernel pointers leak. KASLR dies.

The fix

The upstream commit changes two lines:

kfree_rcu() queues the free to happen after the RCU grace period. Any concurrent reader on another CPU finishes its RCU read-side critical section before the memory is actually freed. The race window closes.

That struct rcu_head rcu field in ip_options_rcu finally gets used for what it was put there for.

The proof

KASAN (Kernel Address Sanitizer) catches the UAF cleanly. With a KASAN-enabled kernel (6.12.112), the PoC produces this within seconds:

The UAF reads the ip_options_rcu object at the first byte (optlen field in the ip_options struct). The allocation trace shows tcp_v4_route_req -> tcp_conn_request – the IP options are allocated during SYN processing when the kernel echoes the client’s Record Route option.

The free trace shows kfree -> inet_sock_destruct -> __sk_destruct -> tcp_v4_rcv. Socket destruction frees the IP options with kfree() instead of kfree_rcu(), leaving a window where concurrent RCU readers on other CPUs can access the freed kmalloc-96 object.

The object is a 96-byte slab allocation – struct ip_options_rcu contains a 4-byte struct rcu_head plus the variable-length struct ip_options with the Record Route data (39 bytes of option data + padding to the next 8-byte boundary).

Detection

Network-level: the exploit requires TCP SYN packets with IP options. Normal internet traffic almost never carries IP options. Any burst of SYNs with ip.hdr_len > 20 from a single source is suspicious. Suricata rules in the repo.

Kernel-level: KASAN reports mentioning ip_options_build in the read trace and inet_sock_destruct in the free trace. Sigma rule in the repo.

Immediate mitigation (drops all TCP with IP options):

This works because almost nothing legitimate uses IP options anymore. The Record Route and Timestamp options were designed for network diagnostics in the 1980s. Modern traceroute uses UDP or ICMP, not IP options. Dropping them at the firewall is a zero-impact mitigation for almost every deployment.

Affected versions

The vulnerable commit (079096f103fa – “tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests into ehash table”) was merged in Linux 4.4. The fix landed in these stable releases:

SeriesFixed in
5.10.x5.10.272
5.15.x5.15.223
6.1.x6.1.190
6.6.x6.6.159
6.12.x6.12.113
6.18.x6.18.56
7.2.x7.2.10
mainline7.3

If you’re running any Linux kernel from 4.4 through the pre-fix version of your series, you’re vulnerable. Every distro, every cloud provider, every container host. The only requirement is an open TCP port, which every server has.

Timeline

  • 2016: Vulnerable commit 079096f103fa merged (Linux 4.4)
  • 2026-10: Anthropic AI discovers the vulnerability using Claude
  • 2026-10: Patch submitted and merged upstream
  • 2026-10: Stable releases with fix start shipping
  • 2026-10-28: THN, Red Hat, Ostorlab publish advisories
  • 2026-11-01: This analysis and PoC published

Reproduction

The PoC opens race windows by completing TCP handshakes with Record Route IP options, immediately RST-ing the connection, and retransmitting the original SYN. Each iteration takes milliseconds. KASAN reports typically appear within the first 50 attempts on a 4-core VM.
entry.summary: CVE-2026-98432: a race condition in the Linux kernel's TCP/IPv4 stack turns a 2-line kfree vs kfree_rcu mistake into remote pre-auth kernel code execution. Affects every Linux kernel from 4.4 to present. CVSS 9.8. The attacker sends a SYN with IP options, completes the handshake, destroys the socket, and retransmits. Lost races cost nothing. I wrote a PoC, detection rules, and traced the full exploitation chain.

Every page on a YOOtheme Pro site hands you a signed image URL. The signature is supposed to prevent abuse of the image transformation handler. It doesn’t cover the FROMFILE or SAVE parameters. One GET request, and the handler fetches a JPEG/PHP polyglot from your server, traverses out of the cache directory, and writes it wherever you want. PHP executes it on the next hit.

CVSS 10.0. Pre-auth. One request. No cookies, no tokens, no login. The target’s own image handler signs your webshell delivery for you.

I started looking at this after Unit 42 dropped their advisory on October 26 confirming active exploitation. By then, automated scanners had already been planting webshells for days. The fix (5.0.53) shipped October 21, but commercial WordPress/Joomla themes don’t auto-update like core plugins. A lot of sites are still running 5.0.52 or older.

CVE-2026-102785. CWE-434. CVSS 10.0 Critical. PoC, check script, detection rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-102785.

Background: YOOtheme Pro’s image handler

YOOtheme Pro is a premium theme framework for WordPress and Joomla. It’s the kind of product agencies use: visual page builder, UIkit-based components, production-grade caching. One of its features is on-the-fly image transformation. Instead of generating thumbnails at upload time, YOOtheme serves images through a handler that resizes, crops, and converts them on request.

The handler URLs look like this on WordPress:

Or in path-based mode:

The hash parameter is a signature. It’s supposed to ensure that only legitimate image transformation requests get processed. The handler checks the hash, loads the source image, applies transformations, writes the result to the cache directory, and serves it.

Every page on a YOOtheme site includes these signed URLs in <img> tags, CSS backgrounds, and OpenGraph metadata. They’re public by design. You need them to be public so browsers can load the images.

The vulnerable code path

The signature validation has a gap. The handler accepts two parameters that aren’t bound to the hash:

FROMFILE: instead of loading the source image from the local filesystem, fetch it from an arbitrary URL. This is how the handler was meant to support remote image sources during development. It was never removed.

SAVE: instead of writing the result to the standard cache path derived from the signed URL, write it to a custom path. This parameter allows path traversal.

Here’s the sequence:

The handler validates the hash against the original route and image parameters. It passes. Then it reads FROMFILE, fetches the attacker’s image, processes it, and writes the result to the SAVE path. The hash never covered FROMFILE or SAVE.

The fix in 5.0.53 restricts the operation list to a fixed allowlist: type, crop, resize, rotate, flip, thumbnail. Anything else (including FROMFILE and SAVE) is rejected. The cache filename is also validated against the signed URL, so even if you could sneak an operation through, the output path can’t deviate.

The polyglot: PHP inside a JPEG

The handler doesn’t just copy the file from FROMFILE. It processes it as an image: loads it with GD or Imagick, applies any transformations in the route, and re-encodes it before writing. Sticking <?php at the end of a JPEG would get stripped.

But IPTC metadata survives.

JPEG files can carry IPTC-IIM data in the APP13 marker (0xFFED). This is the standard metadata format for photo captions, credits, and copyright notices. Both GD and Imagick are designed to preserve IPTC during re-encoding. It’s a feature, not a bug, from the image library’s perspective. Photographers and news agencies rely on this metadata surviving edits.

The polyglot payload is a valid JPEG image with PHP code embedded in the IPTC Caption field (record 2, dataset 120, tag \x1c\x02\x78). The JPEG renders normally as an image. But when saved with a .php extension and accessed through a web server, PHP scans the binary content for <?php tags, finds the one inside the IPTC data, and executes it.

Building the polyglot:

  1. Start with a valid JPEG (any size, any content)
  2. Add an APP13 marker containing a Photoshop 3.0 resource block
  3. Inside the resource block, write an IPTC record with the PHP payload in the Caption field
  4. The result is simultaneously a valid JPEG (opens in any viewer) and valid PHP (executes the embedded code)

The PHP shell I use is minimal: it reads a c parameter from the request, passes it to system(), and wraps the output with markers so the PoC script can extract it cleanly.

Walking the exploit

The full attack takes one GET request from the attacker’s browser or script. Here’s what happens end to end:

Step 1: Harvest a signed URL. Visit any page on the target site. Every page includes signed image URLs in the HTML. Extract one. The attacker needs the hash parameter and the route structure. Both are public.

Step 2: Build the polyglot. Generate a JPEG/PHP polyglot with a command-execution shell in the IPTC Caption field. Host it on a server the target can reach.

Step 3: Start a payload server. The target’s image handler needs to fetch the polyglot. The attacker runs a simple HTTP server:

Step 4: Fire the exploit. Rebuild the signed URL, keeping the original hash, and append the two extra parameters:

The handler receives the request. It validates hash against the route (passes, because we kept the original hash). It reads FROMFILE, makes an HTTP request to the attacker’s server, downloads the polyglot. It processes the image (IPTC survives). It reads SAVE, traverses ../../ out of the cache directory into wp-content/uploads/, and writes shell.php.

Step 5: Execute. POST to the shell with c=id:

That’s www-data running commands on the web server. From a single unauthenticated GET request.

The proof

Against a test installation running YOOtheme Pro 5.0.49 on WordPress:

Reading files:

The check script detects the vulnerability without triggering it:

Negative control

Against a patched installation (5.0.53), the signature reuse probe returns 400:

The fix in 5.0.53 does two things: restricts the handler to a fixed operation allowlist (no more FROMFILE/SAVE), and validates the output filename against the signed URL. Both blocks work independently.

Impact

This is bad. Here’s why:

The vulnerability is pre-auth. No credentials, no cookies, no API keys. Every visitor to a YOOtheme site has everything they need to exploit it: a signed image URL from the page source.

The exploit is one GET request. Not a race condition, not a chain of three bugs, not a timing attack. One request writes a webshell.

YOOtheme Pro is a premium product used by agencies and commercial sites. Exact install counts aren’t public, but the framework has been actively maintained since YOOtheme 4 and is widely deployed. Both WordPress and Joomla are affected.

The patch shipped October 21 but commercial themes don’t auto-update. Site owners have to manually update or use a premium update plugin. Unit 42 confirmed in-the-wild exploitation on October 26. That’s a 5-day window where the patch existed but attackers were already scanning.

Known IOCs from the wild: webshell filenames matching yt + 7 hex characters in wp-content/uploads/, ALFA_DATA directories dropped alongside the webshells, traffic from 168.144.251.199.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Signature reuse on image handlerProvenRenamed route accepted with original hash
Pre-auth exploitationProvenZero credentials, one GET request
FROMFILE fetches from attacker URLProvenPayload server receives request from target
SAVE traverses out of cache dirProvenPHP file written to wp-content/uploads/
JPEG/PHP polyglot survives re-encodingProvenPHP code in IPTC metadata executes after processing
Remote code executionProvenid command output extracted from webshell
Patched version safeConfirmedSignature rejected on 5.0.53
In-the-wild exploitationConfirmedUnit 42 advisory (Oct 26, 2026)

Detection

Network-level (Suricata): watch for FROMFILE and SAVE parameters in requests containing hash=. These parameters don’t appear in legitimate YOOtheme image handler traffic. The combined FROMFILE + SAVE + hash= pattern is high-confidence.

Host-level (Sigma): PHP files appearing in wp-content/uploads/ or Joomla images/ directories (especially files matching yt[hex]{7}.php), POST requests to those files, and ALFA_DATA directory creation.

Both rule sets: detection/ in the repo.

The Asenka Guard WordPress plugin also scans for suspicious PHP files in upload and YOOtheme cache paths. Worth deploying alongside the update if you’re doing incident response.

The fix

Upgrade to YOOtheme Pro 5.0.53 or later. That’s it. There’s no workaround, no configuration toggle, no WAF rule that reliably blocks all variants (the reference PoC by antid00t includes 13 WAF bypass profiles with parameter randomization and HTTP parameter pollution).

What 5.0.53 changed:

  1. The image handler now only accepts operations from a fixed list: type, crop, resize, rotate, flip, thumbnail. Everything else is rejected before processing.
  2. The output cache filename is validated against the signed URL. Even if an operation slipped through, the output path can’t deviate from what was signed.

Both changes together make the attack impossible. The first blocks the FROMFILE/SAVE injection. The second blocks the path traversal.

Timeline

DateEvent
2026-10-21YOOtheme Pro 5.0.53 released with fix
2026-10-23CVE-2026-102785 published by Joomla CNA
2026-10-24First public reference PoC (antid00t)
2026-10-26Unit 42 confirms active exploitation in the wild
2026-10-27This analysis and PoC published

Credit to David Willis-Owen for the original discovery and disclosure.

Reproduction

YOOtheme Pro is commercial software, so there’s no Docker lab in this repo. You need your own installation. The exploit requires the target to make an outbound HTTP request to your payload server, so pass --lhost with an IP the target can reach.

Readers running YOOtheme Pro: update to 5.0.53 now. Check your wp-content/uploads/ directory for files matching yt*.php. If you find them, you’ve already been hit.

Grab any public signed image URL, add FROMFILE + SAVE with path traversal, and the handler writes a JPEG/PHP polyglot webshell for you. CVSS 10.0, actively exploited.

Every Linux machine running ksmbd with a guest share has 28 bytes of kernel heap memory waiting to walk out the door. No credentials. No RDMA hardware. One TCP connection to port 445 is enough. The attacker sends a burst of SMB1 packets followed by a single SMB2 ECHO, and the kernel copies whatever was sitting next to the request buffer in the SLAB allocator into the response and sends it back over the wire: pointers, KASAN redzone markers, fragments of other connections’ data, anything that happened to be in kmalloc-64 at the time.

I found this vulnerability (ZDI-CAN-33774, CVSS 9.0) while studying the ksmbd protocol negotiation path after my work on ZDI-CAN-33549. The same subsystem, same maintainer, same CVSS score, but a completely different bug class: this time it is a TOCTOU race condition in the protocol handler dispatch, not an integer underflow in the RDMA path.

Background: How ksmbd Dispatches Protocol Handlers

ksmbd is the in-kernel SMB server for Linux, an alternative to the userspace Samba daemon. It implements both SMB1 (the legacy protocol) and SMB2/3 (the modern protocol) and needs to handle clients that start with an SMB1 multi-protocol negotiate before upgrading to SMB2. This means the server must be able to switch protocol handlers mid-connection.

The protocol handlers live in a dispatch table called conn->ops. This struct contains function pointers for every protocol-specific operation: building response headers, checking sessions, verifying signatures, parsing commands. There are two tables: smb1_server_ops (6 function pointers, handles 35+ byte SMB1 PDUs) and smb2_server_ops (full set, expects 64+ byte SMB2 headers).

The negotiation flow works like this: a connection thread sits in ksmbd_conn_handler_loop() reading PDUs off the socket. For each PDU, it calls queue_ksmbd_work(), which does two things in sequence:

  1. Calls ksmbd_init_smb_server(conn) to inspect the PDU’s protocol magic (\xFF SMB for SMB1, \xFE SMB for SMB2) and set conn->ops to the matching dispatch table
  2. Allocates a work item, binds work->request_buf to the PDU buffer, and queues it for a kworker thread to process

A separate kworker thread picks up the work item later and calls conn->ops->init_rsp_hdr(work) to build the response header, then conn->ops->check_user_session(work) to validate the session.

Here is the fundamental problem: the request buffer is saved per-work, but conn->ops is read from the shared connection struct at dequeue time. If another PDU arrives and changes conn->ops between enqueue and dequeue, the kworker runs the wrong handler on the wrong buffer. A 40-byte SMB1 buffer gets processed by an SMB2 handler that expects at least 64 bytes.

Why kmalloc-64 Matters

Understanding the SLAB allocator layout makes the leak concrete. The kernel’s SLUB allocator groups small allocations into per-size caches: kmalloc-8, kmalloc-16, kmalloc-32, kmalloc-64, kmalloc-128, and so on. A 40-byte allocation lands in kmalloc-64 because 64 is the next power-of-two bucket. The object gets the first 40 bytes; the remaining 24 bytes of the 64-byte slot are padding.

With KASAN enabled, those 24 padding bytes are poisoned with 0xFC (the SLUB_RED_ACTIVE marker). Without KASAN, they are whatever the previous occupant of that slot left behind. The 4 bytes at offset 64..67 belong to the next kmalloc-64 object entirely, a completely separate kernel allocation that could be holding a file descriptor table, a network buffer, or a work item from another subsystem.

When init_smb2_rsp_hdr() reads offsets 40 through 67, it reads: 24 bytes of same-slot padding (or KASAN redzone) plus 4 bytes from the neighboring object. All 28 bytes are copied into the SMB2 error response and sent to the attacker. On a production kernel without KASAN, those “padding” bytes are stale data from a recently freed object: potentially function pointers that reveal the kernel text base, heap addresses that map the SLAB layout, or fragments of other users’ SMB session data.

The Vulnerable Code

In fs/smb/server/server.c, queue_ksmbd_work():

In the kworker, __handle_ksmbd_work():

The ops selection in smb_common.c:

When init_smb2_rsp_hdr() runs on an SMB1 buffer, it reads fields that do not exist in the allocation:

A 35-byte SMB1 PDU allocates pdu_size + 4 + 1 = 40 bytes (connection.c:511-512) in kmalloc-64. The SMB2 handler reads up to offset 67. That is 28 bytes past the 40-byte allocation boundary, into the SLAB redzone and adjacent objects.

The Trigger: Not a Tight Instruction Race

This is not a nanosecond-precision race between two CPU cores fighting over a cacheline. The window is wide and the trigger is reliable.

One write(2) call delivers a single TCP segment containing 64 short SMB1 PDUs (35 bytes each, RFC1002-framed to 39 bytes on the wire) followed by one SMB2 ECHO (68 bytes, framed to 72). The total payload is about 2.5 KB. The connection thread reads all of them from the kernel’s TCP receive buffer without blocking on the socket, because they all arrived in one segment. It queues the 64 SMB1 works with conn->ops = smb1_server_ops, then processes the ECHO. The ECHO triggers init_smb3_11_server(), which stores conn->ops = smb2_server_ops.

At this point, every SMB1 work still sitting in the workqueue will execute init_smb2_rsp_hdr(). The connection thread has already moved on, but the kworkers have not caught up yet. The window is the entire time between “last SMB1 work queued” and “all kworkers have read conn->ops”, which can be milliseconds.

In testing, 30-40% of the burst consistently triggers the confusion. Over 500 iterations with 64-PDU bursts, the PoC produces roughly 6000 leaks per connection.

Two details keep the trigger clean:

  • The SMB1 PDUs use command byte 0x00, not 0x72 (NEGOTIATE). ksmbd_verify_smb_message() returns -EINVAL at smb_common.c:171 before incrementing outstanding_credits, so the connection does not strangle itself on the credit limit. The server sees “bad command, skip it” and moves on.
  • The SMB2 ECHO (command 0x000d) is one of three session-free opcodes (NEGOTIATE, SESSION_SETUP, ECHO). It does not require a valid session, so it processes cleanly even on a fresh connection and triggers the ops flip.

Lab Topology and Traffic Flow

The PoC runs inside a QEMU VM alongside ksmbd. The traffic is real TCP over the VM’s network stack, hitting the same kernel code path a remote attacker would:

The PoC binary (opsflip) itself only needs a TCP socket, so it works remotely too. The verify script reads dmesg for KASAN evidence, which requires running on the target.

Walking the Exploit

Step 1: Connect. The attacker opens a raw TCP connection to port 445. No SMB negotiate handshake, no session setup, no authentication. The connection thread starts with conn->need_neg = true, which means every PDU triggers a call to ksmbd_init_smb_server() to re-select the protocol handler.

Step 2: Build the burst. 64 SMB1 PDUs of 35 bytes each. The protocol magic is \xFF S M B, command 0x00, PidHigh set to 0x0002 (which maps to SMB2_LOGOFF_HE when the buffer is misread as an SMB2 header). This command choice is deliberate: it makes smb2_check_user_session() return -EIO immediately (the connection is not authenticated), which triggers the error response path that carries the leaked bytes.

Step 3: Append the flip trigger. One 68-byte SMB2 ECHO (\xFE S M B, StructureSize 64, command 0x000d). This is a legal SMB2 PDU that passes the pdu_size >= 66 check at connection.c:549. It exists only to make the connection thread run init_smb3_11_server() and overwrite conn->ops.

Step 4: Send everything in one write(2). The kernel’s TCP stack delivers the entire payload to the ksmbd connection thread’s socket buffer. The thread parses PDU by PDU: queue work for SMB1 #1, queue work for SMB1 #2, …, queue work for SMB1 #64, then hit the ECHO and flip conn->ops. All 64 SMB1 works are now in the workqueue with the wrong handler.

Step 5: The kworkers process the confusion. Each confused SMB1 work runs init_smb2_rsp_hdr(). The function copies rcv_hdr->Id.SyncId.TreeId from buffer offset 40 (4 bytes past the allocation), rcv_hdr->SessionId from offset 44 (8 bytes), and rcv_hdr->Signature from offset 52 (16 bytes). All 28 bytes come from whatever lives in the adjacent SLAB memory.

Step 6: The leak walks out. The confused work fails smb2_check_user_session() with -EIO (the connection has no valid session) and init_smb2_rsp_hdr() copies the response header (including the leaked fields) into a 77-byte SMB2 error response. The response is sent back to the attacker over TCP. The attacker reads the SessionId and Signature fields from the response to extract the 24 leaked bytes (plus 4 from TreeId).

An important oracle: a work that was NOT confused (stays with SMB1 handlers) triggers set_smb1_rsp_status(), which sets send_no_response = true. The server sends nothing back. So any 77-byte SMB2 error reply on this connection is proof that the flip happened and the OOB read occurred. The attacker does not need KASAN or dmesg access to confirm exploitation; the response itself is the evidence.

What Comes Back in the Reply

The 77-byte SMB2 error response has a fixed structure: 4-byte RFC1002 length, 64-byte SMB2 header, 9-byte error body. The leaked bytes sit in three header fields:

  • TreeId (4 bytes at header offset 36): maps to buffer offset 40..43, the first 4 bytes past the allocation
  • SessionId (8 bytes at header offset 40): maps to buffer offset 44..51
  • Signature (16 bytes at header offset 48): maps to buffer offset 52..67, extending 3 bytes into the next SLAB object

On a KASAN kernel, these fields contain 0x00 (in-object padding) and 0xFC (redzone poison). On a production kernel, they contain whatever the SLAB allocator left in those bytes: stale heap pointers from freed objects, fragments of recently deallocated network buffers, partial contents of other connections’ request data. Each trigger attempt reads a different snapshot of the heap neighborhood, because the SLAB allocator recycles slots and different objects occupy the adjacent positions at different times.

The Crash (Proof)

KASAN catches the out-of-bounds read in init_smb2_rsp_hdr:

The allocation is 40 bytes in kmalloc-64. The read at ffff8880222c2ba8 is exactly at the boundary (0 bytes to the right of the 40-byte region), confirming the 28-byte overread into the SLAB redzone and neighboring objects.

The leaked bytes show up on the wire. Here are actual samples from the PoC:

The 0xfc bytes are KASAN’s slab redzone poison (SLUB_RED_ACTIVE). On a kernel without KASAN, those bytes would contain live heap data from adjacent allocations: function pointers, buffer contents from other connections, freed object metadata. Each attempt reads a different slice of whatever the allocator placed next to the request buffer.

Negative Control

Same payload on a patched kernel (commit 68f410faedaf):

Zero leaks. Zero KASAN reports. The wait_event() drains all queued work before reading the next PDU, preventing the ops flip entirely. The patched connection thread blocks until req_running drops to zero after each negotiation-phase PDU.

Impact

This is a pre-auth kernel heap information disclosure with a path to worse.

The attacker needs only TCP connectivity to port 445 and a guest share on the target (a common default). Zero credentials are required. Each trigger attempt leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap. Over thousands of iterations (the PoC runs 32,000 per connection by default), the attacker can:

  • Map heap layout: leak kmalloc-64 SLAB object addresses, defeating kernel ASLR
  • Read kernel pointers: function pointers from freed objects reveal kernel text base
  • Harvest cross-connection data: other sessions’ metadata, partial SMB buffers, authentication tokens sitting in adjacent SLAB objects

The comparison with ZDI-CAN-33549 is worth making explicit. That bug needed RDMA hardware (InfiniBand, RoCE, or soft-RoCE) and SMB2 authentication to reach the vulnerable code path. This one needs nothing but TCP. ZDI-CAN-33549 wrote attacker-controlled data past the buffer (OOB write, heap corruption, kernel crash). This one reads kernel data past the buffer and sends it to the attacker (OOB read, information disclosure). In a multi-stage attack, you would use ZDI-CAN-33774 first to leak heap layout and defeat KASLR, then use ZDI-CAN-33549 (or the documented OOB write path in this bug) to achieve controlled corruption. Together they cover the full read-then-write primitive that kernel exploitation chains typically require.

The vulnerability report also documents two additional paths from the same race:

  1. OOB write via smb2_set_info -> parse_sec_desc: if the confused work reaches the SET_INFO handler instead of failing at check_user_session, the attacker’s data is written past the buffer. This PoC does not exercise this path.
  2. NULL dereference via conn->ops->is_sign_req: smb1_server_ops does not define is_sign_req. If conn->ops flips back to SMB1 between check_user_session (server.c:202) and the is_sign_req check (server.c:210), the kworker calls a NULL function pointer and oopses. This is a denial of service.

RCENot provenInfo leak + OOB write path demonstrates mechanism; RCE theoretical

Detection

Network (Suricata): The exploit sends rapid SMB1/SMB2 protocol interleaving on a single connection, which never happens in legitimate SMB negotiation. A legitimate client completes SMB1 negotiation before switching to SMB2 and never interleaves the two. A detection rule is in the repository.

Host (kernel logs): Look for KASAN reports in init_smb2_rsp_hdr:

A Sigma rule for kernel log detection is in the repository.

The Fix

Commit 68f410faedaf by Namjae Jeon adds 5 lines to queue_ksmbd_work():

When the connection is new or still negotiating, the thread waits for all queued work to complete before reading the next PDU. This ensures conn->ops cannot be flipped while earlier works are still in-flight. After negotiation completes and need_neg is cleared, PDUs pipeline normally with no performance impact.

The fix correctly targets the negotiation window: it serializes only the first few PDUs on a connection (where the protocol switch happens) and returns to full pipelining once the protocol is established. The performance cost is minimal because the wait_event() only fires while need_neg is true, which lasts for exactly the first one or two PDUs on every connection.

An alternative fix would be to save conn->ops per-work-item at enqueue time, so each kworker uses the ops table that was current when its request was queued. That approach would be more general (it would prevent any future TOCTOU through conn->ops) but would require changes to every callsite in __handle_ksmbd_work(). The chosen fix is simpler and narrower: it eliminates the race by preventing the scenario where the connection thread can modify conn->ops while work items from a previous protocol are still in flight.

The root cause is a design pattern that appears in other network subsystems too: a per-connection dispatch table modified by the receive path while workers from earlier receives are still active. Any time a server supports protocol upgrades or multi-protocol negotiation with a shared handler table and asynchronous work queues, this class of bug is possible.

The fix is in the ksmbd maintainer tree but has not reached mainline as of October 24, 2026.

PHP ships session.upload_progress.enabled turned on by default. Every version, every installation. If your server’s php.ini uses php_serialize for sessions and any endpoint switches to the php handler at runtime before session_start(), an unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary PHP objects into your session file. No credentials. No cookies. One multipart POST with a pipe character in the right form field.

I was reading through the PHP2Shell patches (CVE-2026-109618/109619, dropped October 21) when I noticed the fix only covered the filename field in multipart uploads. The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS value goes through the exact same rfc1867 callback, lands in the same session file, and nobody sanitizes it either. I started writing a PoC that night.

Two days later, php.net quietly put out a mitigation advisory. No patch. The entire recommendation is “set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini.” For a pre-auth RCE. In 2026.

CVE-2026-115560. CVSS 9.8 Critical. Unpatched. PoC, check script, detection rules: al4n4n/achilles-heel/CVE-2026-115560.

Background: PHP session serialization handlers

PHP has three session serialization handlers, and the mismatch between them has been a known class of bug since at least 2015. What makes this CVE different from the textbook version is the attack surface: you don’t need authentication, you don’t need the application to accept user input into sessions, and you don’t even need cookies.

The three handlers store the same session data in incompatible formats:

php (legacy): key|serialized_value. The pipe | separates the key name from the serialized value. This is the oldest format and still the default on many installations.

php_serialize: Standard serialize() for the entire session array. No pipe delimiter. The whole thing is one serialized string. Modern PHP docs recommend this one.

php_binary: Length-prefixed binary encoding. Rarely seen in the wild, but also mismatches with the others.

The fundamental problem: if one handler writes and a different handler reads, the data gets reinterpreted. When php_serialize writes a session containing upload_progress_PAYLOAD|O:9:... as a key name, the string |O:9:... is just part of that key. But when the php handler reads the same file, it scans for | as a delimiter, finds the one inside our key, and passes everything to the right of it straight into unserialize().

The pipe character is data to one handler and a delimiter to another. That’s the entire bug.

The attack surface: session.upload_progress

Handler mismatches have been known for years, but exploiting them usually required the application to write attacker-controlled data into $_SESSION. That limits the attack surface to authenticated users or specific input flows.

session.upload_progress removes that limitation entirely.

When enabled (it is, by default, on every PHP installation since 5.4), PHP’s rfc1867 multipart form handler automatically writes upload progress information into the session. The session key is upload_progress_<value> where <value> comes directly from a POST field named PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. The attacker controls that value. No sanitization, no length limit, no character filtering.

Here’s what PHP’s rfc1867 callback does during a multipart upload, before your application code even runs:

  1. Reads PHPSESSID from the POST body (from the body, not just cookies, regardless of session.use_only_cookies)
  2. Creates or opens the session file with that ID
  3. Writes upload_progress_<PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS value> to the session file
  4. Uses the server-configured handler for serialization (because application code hasn’t had a chance to call ini_set() yet)

Step 4 is where it falls apart. The rfc1867 callback runs pre-RINIT, before any PHP userland code executes. Your ini_set('session.serialize_handler', 'php') in index.php changes nothing about what the upload handler writes. It writes with whatever php.ini says. But when your code later calls session_start(), it reads with the handler you just switched to.

Two different handlers. Same file. The attacker controls what’s in between.

The vulnerable pattern

Three conditions have to line up. Here’s what they look like in practice:

And the server’s php.ini:

Important caveat: this PoC uses a synthetic LabGadget class that I planted in the lab specifically to demonstrate RCE. No real application ships a class that blindly calls shell_exec() from a property. In a real attack, you’d need to find a usable gadget chain in whatever framework the target runs. The PHPGGC project maintains chains for most major PHP frameworks, but finding one that’s autoloaded at the right moment is application-specific work.

What is real: the object injection primitive. If the three preconditions are met, arbitrary objects go into unserialize(). The gadget chain determines what happens next.

Where does the handler-switching pattern appear in the wild? Legacy codebases that migrated from php to php_serialize at the config level but kept ini_set() in their bootstrap code. Framework configurations where the server and application disagree on the handler. Multi-tenant setups where the vhost config uses one handler and the application uses another. It’s not universal, but it’s not rare either.

Walking the exploit

The exploit is a race between two threads hitting the same session file.

Thread 1 (producer): sends a slow multipart POST to the handler-switching endpoint. The POST body carries three fields:

Why the trickle? PHP deletes upload progress data from the session when the upload finishes (session.upload_progress.cleanup = 1). By sending the file body one 16KB chunk at a time with 150ms between them, we hold the session file open for ~2.5 seconds. That’s our race window.

Why PHPSESSID in the POST body? The rfc1867 handler reads it from the multipart fields before session.use_only_cookies takes effect. The attacker picks the session ID, no cookies needed.

The rfc1867 callback writes this to /tmp/sess_attacker_controlled_session_id using php_serialize:

To php_serialize, the | is just part of the string. Nothing special.

Thread 2 (consumer): fires rapid GET requests to the same endpoint with Cookie: PHPSESSID=attacker_controlled_session_id. Each request runs:

Now the php handler reads the file. It scans left to right for |, finds the one we planted, and splits there. Everything to the right goes into unserialize():

PHP creates a LabGadget instance with $cmd = "id". The deserialization itself fails partway through (the rest of the session data doesn’t parse cleanly under the php handler), but that doesn’t matter. PHP_VAR_UNSERIALIZE_DESTROY runs destructors on every object created during the attempt, even on failure. __destruct() fires, shell_exec("id") runs, and the output lands in a web-accessible drop file.

The consumer thread fires maybe 40-60 requests during the 2.5-second window. Only one needs to hit while the session file exists on disk.

The proof

Against the lab target (PHP 8.4.27-apache with the synthetic LabGadget class and the handler-switching index.php):

That uid=33(www-data) is the output of id running as the Apache worker process inside the container. No credentials sent. No cookies (the session ID came from the POST body). One multipart form, one pipe character.

Reading arbitrary files:

To be clear about what this proves: the object injection primitive (getting attacker-controlled data into unserialize() without authentication) is real and not specific to the lab. The RCE part depends on the LabGadget class that I put there. A real target would need a real gadget chain.

Negative control

The mitigated container has session.upload_progress.enabled = 0:

The handler mismatch still exists, but the rfc1867 callback never fires, so there’s no way to inject data into the session pre-RINIT. The exploit fails on every round.

The noswitch.php endpoint (same gadget class, no ini_set() switch) is also immune. When the same handler reads and writes, the pipe character stays inside the serialized string where it belongs.

Impact

Let me be honest about the blast radius. This is not “every PHP server is vulnerable.” Three things have to line up:

  1. Server-side handler set to php_serialize or php_binary in php.ini. Many modern setups do this (the PHP docs recommend php_serialize), but it’s a configuration choice, not the default.
  2. Application code switches the handler to php at runtime via ini_set() before session_start(). This is the narrowest requirement. It shows up in legacy codebases and certain framework configurations, but most applications don’t do this.
  3. session.upload_progress.enabled = 1. This is the default. Almost nobody turns it off.

If all three are present, the attacker gets arbitrary object injection without authentication. The actual impact then depends on a fourth factor: whether there’s a usable gadget chain (a class with an exploitable __destruct() or __wakeup()) autoloaded at the time of deserialization.

In the lab, that’s LabGadget, a class I wrote specifically for this PoC with shell_exec() in __destruct(). It doesn’t exist in the real world. For real targets, the PHPGGC project catalogs gadget chains for Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, Drupal, Magento, and dozens of other frameworks. Finding one that works is application-specific, but it’s a solved problem for many popular stacks.

ClaimStatusEvidence
Serialize handler mismatchProvenServer: php_serialize, runtime: php
Pre-auth object injectionProvenZero credentials, session ID from POST body
RCE via synthetic gadgetProvenid output extracted from lab drop file
Race condition exploitableProvenProducer/consumer threads, ~47 hits in 2.5s window
Mitigation effectiveConfirmedupload_progress=0 prevents exploitation
RCE on real-world appsNot provenLab gadget is synthetic; real apps need real chains
Handler switch pattern in the wildNot provenKnown to exist but prevalence not measured

Detection

Network-level (Suricata): look for multipart POST requests where PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS contains |O: (pipe followed by serialized object notation). The detection rule also flags PHPSESSID delivered via POST body alongside upload progress fields, which is unusual in legitimate traffic.

Host-level (Sigma): PHP error logs containing Failed to decode session object after session_start() indicate the handler mismatch fired. This happens on every exploit attempt, successful or not.

Both rule sets are in the detection/ directory.

The fix (or lack of one)

There is no patch. As of this writing, the only mitigation is:

This goes in php.ini or a conf.d file. You cannot set it via ini_set() in your application code, because the rfc1867 callback registers before your code runs. By the time PHP reaches your ini_set(), the upload handler has already processed the multipart body and written to the session file. The same pre-RINIT timing that makes this exploitable also makes the obvious application-level fix impossible.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, patched October 21, 2026) exploited the filename field in multipart uploads. CVE-2026-115560 uses the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS value field instead, which goes through the same rfc1867 callback but a different code path. The PHP2Shell patches don’t touch it.

A real fix would need to do one of two things: sanitize the upload progress value before writing it to the session (strip or escape characters that could be misinterpreted by other handlers), or tag session files with the handler that wrote them and refuse to read with a different one. Neither approach exists in any released or proposed patch.

2026-10-23CVE-2026-115560 disclosed, php.net publishes mitigation advisory

2026-10-24This analysis and PoC published

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post by running the commands above. The lab uses Docker, the exploit uses Python stdlib only, and the entire thing takes under a minute.
